lessons.summary: The garbage collector is not a mystery box you tune with flags; it is a cost you create, one allocation at a time. This sector makes that cost visible: bytes per operation, gen0 collections, the 85,000-byte cliff, pooled buffers, weak caches, and why a finalizer is the most expensive thing you can add to a type.

# V3·C1 — The GC, generations, and allocation pressure you can see

You have been allocating since your first `new`. Every list you grew, every
string you concatenated, every LINQ chain that materialised a lambda closure
put bytes on the managed heap, and something quietly took them away again. In
the earlier sectors that was the right level of ignorance: correctness first.
This sector removes it. Not so you can "tune the GC" — you almost never
should — but because the size of your programs' allocation rate is a number you
control, and it is the number behind most of the .NET performance work that
actually pays.

The mental model to throw away is "the GC runs every so often". It does not
run on a timer. It runs when an *allocation* cannot be satisfied from the
current gen0 allocation budget. Your code decides when collections happen, by
allocating. That is the whole causal chain, and it is why "reduce allocations"
and "reduce GC time" are the same sentence.

## Generations, in the only detail you need

The .NET heap is generational because of one empirical observation: most
objects die young. So the collector splits the heap into gen0 (just born),
gen1 (survived one collection), gen2 (survived two, i.e. everything long
lived), plus a separate large object heap for anything at or over 85,000
bytes.

A gen0 collection walks the roots — statics, locals on every thread's stack,
GC handles — finds what is reachable, and *copies the survivors* into gen1.
Nothing is done to the garbage at all. That is the trick: a gen0 collection
costs time proportional to what *survived*, not to what died. A million dead
temporary strings cost the collector nothing. One live cache holding a million
objects costs on every gen2 pass.

Two consequences follow, and they are the ones interviewers are actually
listening for:

- Short-lived garbage is close to free. Allocating a temporary in a loop is
  not automatically a bug.
- Objects that survive gen0 but die shortly afterwards — the *midlife crisis* —
  are the expensive ones, because you paid to copy them and then threw them
  away. Buffers held just slightly too long, caches with no eviction, objects
  parked in a queue for a second: that is where the cost is.

```csharp
long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
DoWork();
long allocated = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before;
```

That single API is the most useful measurement in this sector. It is a running
total maintained by the allocator on the current thread; it does not force a
collection, does not need a profiler, and is exact rather than sampled.

## The other two numbers

`GC.CollectionCount(0)` tells you how many gen0 collections have happened
since the process started. Take it before and after a workload and you have
collections per operation. Note the rule that trips people: a gen2 collection
is also a gen1 and a gen0 collection, so the counts are cumulative upward — if
`CollectionCount(2)` went up by one, `CollectionCount(0)` went up by at least
one too.

`GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true)` is the process-wide version of the
first API. Use the per-thread one in tests: it is not perturbed by whatever
the runtime's background threads are doing.

## Exercise 1 - measuring what a delegate allocates

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex1.cs`. Implement
`AllocationProbe.BytesFor(Action work)` returning the bytes allocated on the
calling thread by `work`, and `AllocationProbe.CompareBuilders(int count)`
returning `(long Naive, long Builder)` for two ways of joining `count`
numbers: `result += i.ToString()` in a loop, versus a `StringBuilder`.

For `count = 200` the naive figure is tens of kilobytes and the builder
figure is under two. The gate asserts the ratio, not the exact bytes.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - counting collections, cumulatively

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex2.cs`. `CollectionWatch.Measure`
captures `GC.CollectionCount` for all three generations either side of an
action and returns a `CollectionDelta(int Gen0, int Gen1, int Gen2)`. Then
implement `CollectionDelta.IsConsistent()`, which encodes the cumulative rule:
`Gen0 >= Gen1 >= Gen2`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - a cache that lets go

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex3.cs`. `WeakCache<TKey, TValue>` maps
keys to `WeakReference<TValue>`. `TryGet` answers false both when the key is
absent and when the target has been collected; `Trim()` removes dead entries
and returns how many it dropped. The gate drops its strong references, forces
a collection, and expects the cache to admit the values are gone.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - the 85,000-byte cliff

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex4.cs`. `HeapPlanner.ArrayBytes(int
elementSize, int length)` computes the 64-bit managed size of an array —
object header plus method table pointer plus length field plus payload,
rounded up to an 8-byte boundary — and `HeapPlanner.Destination(...)` returns
`"LOH"` at or above 85,000 bytes and `"Gen0"` below. Then
`HeapPlanner.MaxElementsInGen0(int elementSize)` answers the practical
question: how many elements fit before you fall off the cliff.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - the allocation you did not write

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex5.cs`. `Totals.SumBoxing` takes
`IEnumerable<object>` and unboxes; `Totals.SumGeneric<T>` takes
`IEnumerable<T>` where `T : INumber<T>` and never boxes. Both must produce the
same answer; the gate measures the bytes each allocates and requires the
generic path to be dramatically cheaper.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - renting instead of allocating

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex6.cs`. `ChunkCopier.CopyThrough`
copies a source array into a destination through a rented buffer of at least
`chunkSize` bytes, returning the buffer in a `finally` and never trusting
`buffer.Length` — the pool may hand you a bigger array than you asked for.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - the most expensive keyword in a type declaration

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex7.cs`. `TrackedHandle` owns a fake
unmanaged handle, implements the dispose pattern with a finalizer, and appends
to a shared log so the gate can see *what ran, in what order*. Disposing must
record `"dispose:managed"` and suppress the finalizer; abandoning the object
must record `"finalize"` after a forced collection.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - parsing without the garbage

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex8.cs`. `SettingsReader.FindValue`
finds one key's value in a `"a=1;b=2;c=3"` string using `ReadOnlySpan<char>`
slicing, allocating at most one string — the answer — and nothing when the key
is absent. `CountPairs` counts entries while allocating nothing at all.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex8
```

## Challenge

`BatchProcessor.Run` puts three ideas together: a pooled buffer, span-based
parsing, and a measured allocation budget. It processes a batch of records
and reports the bytes it allocated and the gen0 collections it caused, and the
gate holds it to a per-record budget that a naive `Split`-and-`ToList`
implementation blows through immediately.

## Review

`review1` comes at generations from the other side: a small simulator. You
implement the promotion rule and the budget rule that decide when the runtime
collects and what moves up, then answer one weak-reference question with it.
Building the collector is the fastest way to stop guessing about it.

# Reading - csharp/v3cc01_gc_generations

## Notes

**The collector runs when you allocate, not when time passes.** The allocator
hands out memory by bumping a pointer inside the current gen0 allocation
context. When the budget for that context is exhausted, the next allocation
triggers a gen0 collection. There is no timer and no periodic sweep. So "my
service pauses every few seconds" is really "my service allocates a gen0
budget every few seconds", and the fix is upstream of any GC setting.

**A collection costs what survives.** Mark-and-compact copies live objects and
fixes up the references to them; dead objects are never touched. This inverts
the intuition from `malloc`/`free`, where freeing costs per object. It is why
a tight loop producing millions of dead temporaries can be fine, and a cache
of a million live objects can be expensive on every gen2 pass even when
nothing in it has changed.

**Gen0 is roughly a CPU cache's worth of memory.** The exact budget is dynamic
and adapts to your behaviour, but the design intent is that a gen0 collection
touches memory that is still hot. Two consequences: allocating small and dying
young stays in cache, and objects that survive get copied to a colder address,
which is a second cost after the copy itself.

**The large object heap is different in three ways.** Anything at or over
85,000 bytes goes there, it is collected only with gen2, and it is not
compacted by default — the runtime keeps a free list instead, so it can
fragment. `GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode` exists to compact it on
demand and is a blunt instrument. Arrays that oscillate around the threshold,
sized from request data, are the classic fragmentation source, and
`ArrayPool` exists largely for them.

**Pinning is fragmentation.** A pinned object — a `fixed` block, an interop
buffer, `GCHandle.Alloc(..., GCHandleType.Pinned)` — cannot be moved by the
compactor, so the collector must work around it. Short pins are fine; a
long-lived pinned buffer sitting in gen0 is a hole the allocator routes around
forever. .NET 5 added the pinned object heap so long-lived pinned buffers can
be segregated deliberately.

**Server GC is not "better".** Workstation GC uses one heap and background
collection tuned for latency. Server GC allocates a heap and a dedicated
collection thread per core, which raises throughput and raises memory use, and
in a container with a low CPU limit it can be actively harmful.
`ServerGarbageCollection` is a deployment decision to measure, not a default
to copy.

## ex1

Really testing: that you can attach a number to an opinion.
`GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread` is a running per-thread total, so a
before/after difference is exact and covers everything the delegate did on
that thread. The classic mistake is reaching for a stopwatch instead and
concluding nothing, because at 200 iterations both versions are sub-millisecond
and the timing is noise while the allocation gap is a clean order of
magnitude. The second mistake is forgetting that `+=` on a string allocates
twice per iteration — the `int.ToString()` and a fresh concatenated string
whose size grows with the loop — which is why the naive figure is quadratic in
`count` while the builder's is linear.

## ex2

Really testing: the cumulative rule. `GC.CollectionCount(n)` counts
collections of generation n *or higher*, so a gen2 collection increments all
three counters. `Gen0 >= Gen1 >= Gen2` therefore always holds, and a delta that
violates it means you read the counters in the wrong order or on the wrong
side of the work. The classic mistake is reporting "two gen1 collections and
zero gen0 collections" and building a conclusion on it. Note also what the
numbers cannot tell you: they count collections, not pause time, and most of a
background gen2 collection runs concurrently with your threads.

## ex3

Really testing: what a weak reference actually promises. `WeakReference<T>`
holds a GC handle that does not count as a root, so the target can be
collected while your dictionary entry survives — which means the entry itself
is the leak if you never trim. `TryGetTarget` is the only correct read: it
takes a strong reference for the duration of the call, so the value cannot be
collected between your check and your use. The classic mistake is an
`IsAlive`-then-`Target` pair, which is a race the runtime is allowed to make
you lose. The gate can only be deterministic because it drops its own strong
references and calls `GC.Collect()`; in production "when" is unknowable, which
is exactly the property a cache wants and a work queue does not.

## ex4

Really testing: that 85,000 bytes is a size of the *allocation*, not of your
payload. On 64-bit an array carries an object header word, a method table
pointer and a length field ahead of the elements, so `int[21248]` is already
over the line even though 21248 x 4 = 84,992. The classic mistake is sizing a
buffer at exactly `85000 / sizeof(T)` and landing on the LOH anyway. The
second is assuming the LOH is slow to allocate: it is not especially, it is
slow to *collect*, because it goes only with gen2 and is not compacted.

## ex5

Really testing: boxing as an allocation you did not type. Every `int` handed
to an `object`-typed parameter becomes a 24-byte heap object on 64-bit — header,
method table pointer, payload, alignment. Over a million elements that is 24 MB
of pure garbage. The generic version with `where T : INumber<T>` is
monomorphised by the JIT for each value type, so the arithmetic happens in
registers and nothing is allocated. The classic mistake is believing generics
alone fix it: a constraint of the non-generic `IComparable` boxes on every
comparison, and so does any interface call made through an interface-typed
variable rather than a constrained generic parameter.

## ex6

Really testing: the pool contract. `ArrayPool<T>.Shared.Rent(n)` returns an
array of *at least* n elements — usually the next power of two — holding
whatever the previous tenant left in it. So you track your own length, you
never treat `buffer.Length` as the payload size, and you return in a `finally`
so an exception does not shrink the pool permanently. The classic mistake is
`Return(buffer, clearArray: false)` for a buffer that held secrets, or worse,
keeping a reference to the buffer after returning it — a use-after-free with a
managed accent: two pieces of code writing one array, no exception, corrupt
data.

## ex7

Really testing: why a finalizer costs even when it never runs. A type with a
finalizer is registered on the finalization queue at allocation, cannot be
reclaimed in the gen0 pass that first finds it unreachable — the finalizer
thread must run first — and therefore survives into gen1 or gen2. That is a
guaranteed midlife crisis for every instance. `GC.SuppressFinalize(this)` in
`Dispose` takes it back off the queue, which is why the pattern insists on it.
The classic mistake is a finalizer on a type that owns only managed objects:
it buys nothing, because those objects are collectible anyway, and it makes
every instance more expensive. Modern guidance is to own unmanaged resources
through `SafeHandle` and write no finalizer at all.

## ex8

Really testing: slicing without copying. `ReadOnlySpan<char>` over a string is
a reference and a length; `IndexOf`, `Slice` and comparisons on it allocate
nothing, and `ToString()` at the very end is the one allocation you chose to
make. The classic mistake is `text.Split(';')` at the top of the method, which
allocates an array plus a string per pair before you have decided you need any
of them. The second is trying to store a span in a field or capture it in a
lambda: it is a `ref struct` and the compiler refuses, deliberately — spans are
stack-only so they cannot outlive the memory they view.

## Further reading

- [Fundamentals of garbage collection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals) - generations, budgets, the LOH.
- [The large object heap](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/large-object-heap) - the 85,000-byte threshold and fragmentation.
- [ArrayPool<T>](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.buffers.arraypool-1) - Rent, Return, and the "at least" contract.
- [Cleaning up unmanaged resources](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/unmanaged) - finalizers, SuppressFinalize, SafeHandle.
- [Memory<T> and Span<T> usage guidelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/memory-and-spans/memory-t-usage-guidelines) - what a ref struct may and may not do.
- [Workstation and server GC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/workstation-server-gc) - the deployment decision.

# V3·C1 — The GC, generations, and allocation pressure you can see

## Why this sector exists

There are two ways to talk about the .NET garbage collector. One is folklore:
"the GC handles memory", "call `GC.Collect()` to free memory", "structs are
faster". The other is arithmetic: this operation allocates 4.2 KB, at 10,000
requests per second that is 42 MB/s of gen0 traffic, gen0's budget is a few
megabytes, so we are causing roughly ten collections a second, each costing
what survives. Only the second kind of talk leads anywhere. This sector is
about producing those numbers on your own machine, in a unit test, without a
profiler.

## The model

The managed heap is a bump allocator with a generational collector on top.

- **Allocation** is a pointer increment inside a thread-local allocation
  context, plus zeroing. That is why "allocation is cheap in .NET" is true and
  misleading in the same breath: allocation is cheap, *collection* is the bill.
- **Gen0** holds new objects. When the gen0 budget is exhausted, the next
  allocation triggers a collection: roots are traced, survivors are copied
  into gen1, gen0 resets to empty.
- **Gen1** is a buffer zone. Survivors of a gen1 collection go to gen2.
- **Gen2** is everything long lived, collected rarely, and expensive because
  it traces the whole graph.
- **The LOH** takes allocations of 85,000 bytes or more, is collected only
  with gen2, and is not compacted by default.

Two rules follow directly and are worth memorising as sentences you can say
out loud in a review:

1. A collection costs time proportional to what survives, not to what died.
2. The worst object is the one that survives gen0 and then dies — you paid the
   copy for nothing.

## Measuring, three ways

```csharp
// 1. Bytes, exactly, on this thread. No profiler needed.
long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
Work();
long bytes = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before;

// 2. Collections, cumulative upward.
int g0 = GC.CollectionCount(0), g1 = GC.CollectionCount(1);
Work();
int gen0 = GC.CollectionCount(0) - g0;   // includes gen1 and gen2 passes

// 3. Whole-process totals, useful in a service, noisy in a test.
long total = GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true);
GCMemoryInfo info = GC.GetGCMemoryInfo();   // pause durations, heap sizes
```

`GetGCMemoryInfo().PauseDurations` is the one people miss. It gives you the
actual pause times of recent collections, which is what a latency SLO cares
about — far more useful than a collection count.

## Worked example: where the bytes come from

```csharp
public static string JoinNaive(int count)
{
    string result = "";
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) result += i.ToString();   // two allocs, growing
    return result;
}

public static string JoinBuilder(int count)
{
    var sb = new StringBuilder();
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) sb.Append(i);             // Append(int) does not
    return sb.ToString();                                     // allocate a string
}
```

At `count = 200` the first allocates roughly 60 KB and the second under 2 KB.
The interesting part is not the ratio, it is the shape: the naive version is
O(n^2) in bytes because every `+=` copies the whole accumulated string. Double
the count and the gap quadruples. Note also `sb.Append(i)` rather than
`sb.Append(i.ToString())`: the integer overload formats straight into the
builder's buffer, so the intermediate string never exists.

## Worked example: the boxing you did not type

```csharp
static long SumBoxing(IEnumerable<object> values)   // every int is a 24-byte object
{
    long total = 0;
    foreach (object v in values) total += (int)v;
    return total;
}

static T SumGeneric<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T>
{
    T total = T.Zero;
    foreach (T v in values) total += v;             // no boxing: JIT specialises
    return total;
}
```

Generic math (`INumber<T>`, .NET 7+) is the modern answer to "I want one
numeric routine for `int`, `long` and `decimal` without boxing". The JIT
compiles a separate body per value type, so `total += v` becomes an `add`
instruction rather than an interface call.

## Worked example: renting

```csharp
byte[] buffer = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(chunkSize);
try
{
    int taken = Math.Min(chunkSize, remaining);   // NEVER buffer.Length
    source.AsSpan(offset, taken).CopyTo(buffer);
    destination.AsSpan(offset, taken).Clear();
    buffer.AsSpan(0, taken).CopyTo(destination.AsSpan(offset));
}
finally
{
    ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Return(buffer, clearArray: false);
}
```

Three rules, all of them learned the hard way by somebody:

- `Rent(n)` gives you **at least** n. Track your own length.
- Return in a `finally`, or a thrown exception permanently shrinks the pool.
- After `Return`, the array is not yours. Holding a reference to it is the
  managed equivalent of use-after-free, and it fails silently.

## Common mistakes

- **Calling `GC.Collect()` in production code.** It forces a blocking gen2
  collection, which is the most expensive thing the runtime does, and it
  discards the collector's tuning history. The legitimate uses are a test that
  needs determinism, and a genuine "the process has just finished a huge phase
  and will now idle" moment. That is the whole list.
- **Believing structs never allocate.** A struct in a `List<T>` lives in the
  list's array, on the heap. A struct captured in a lambda lives in a closure
  object, on the heap. A struct cast to an interface is boxed, on the heap.
- **Sizing buffers just under 85,000 bytes** without accounting for the array
  header, and landing on the LOH.
- **Adding a finalizer "just in case".** You have made every instance survive
  an extra generation and added a queue hop, in exchange for nothing.
- **Using `WeakReference` as a memory-pressure valve for things you actually
  need.** A weak cache is a cache whose entries vanish at times you cannot
  predict; if a miss is expensive and unbounded, you wanted a size-bounded
  strong cache instead.
- **Reading `GC.GetTotalMemory(false)` and treating it as "memory used".** It
  is the managed heap's approximate size at that moment, excludes native
  memory entirely, and moves under you.

## Interview answer

*"How does the .NET garbage collector work?"* — Answer in four sentences and
stop. It is a generational, tracing, mark-and-compact collector. Allocation is
a pointer bump in gen0; when gen0's budget is exhausted the next allocation
triggers a collection, which traces from the roots — statics, stack slots, GC
handles — and copies survivors into the next generation, so the cost is
proportional to what lives, not to what died. Gen2 and the large object heap
are collected together and rarely, and the LOH is not compacted by default,
which is why buffers of 85,000 bytes or more want pooling. The practical
consequence is that you control GC time by controlling allocation rate and
object lifetime, not by calling `GC.Collect()`.

If they push further, the differentiating detail is the *midlife crisis*:
objects that survive gen0 and then die are the expensive ones, so the fix for
a service with high gen1 promotion is usually to shorten a lifetime — a buffer
held across an await, a per-request object parked in a queue — rather than to
allocate less overall.

## Check yourself

1. What triggers a gen0 collection?
2. Why is a gen0 collection's cost proportional to survivors rather than to
   garbage?
3. `GC.CollectionCount(2)` increased by 1. What is the minimum you know about
   `GC.CollectionCount(0)`?
4. An `int[]` of what length is the first to land on the LOH on 64-bit?
5. Give three ways a `struct` ends up on the heap.
6. What exactly does `GC.SuppressFinalize(this)` do, and what breaks if you
   omit it from a `Dispose` on a finalizable type?
7. Why does a type with a finalizer survive longer than an equivalent type
   without one, even if the finalizer body is empty?
8. `ArrayPool.Rent(1000)` returned an array with `Length == 1024`. Name two
   bugs that follow from using `Length` as your payload size.
9. When is `WeakReference<T>` the right tool, and when is it a way to make a
   cache miss unpredictable?
10. Why can a `Span<T>` not be a field of a class?
11. What does `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread` include that
    `GC.GetTotalMemory` does not tell you?
12. Your service's p99 latency has periodic spikes. Which single GC number
    would you look at first, and why not collection counts?
13. Why is server GC sometimes worse than workstation GC in a container?
14. What is the midlife crisis, and what code change usually fixes it?

# Long reading - the collector as a cost you author

## The bargain

Automatic memory management is a trade: you give up control of *when* memory
is reclaimed, and in exchange you stop writing use-after-free bugs. The .NET
implementation of that trade is unusually aggressive. It does not reference
count, it does not free objects individually, and it moves your objects behind
your back. Understanding why it made those choices is most of what you need to
predict its behaviour.

Reference counting — the Python and CPython-adjacent approach, and COM's — pays
a small cost on every assignment, cannot collect cycles without a backup
tracer, and gives you deterministic destruction. Tracing pays nothing on
assignment, collects cycles for free, and gives you no determinism at all.
.NET chose tracing, then bolted determinism back on for the cases that need it
via `IDisposable`, which is why the next sector exists.

Having chosen tracing, the runtime chose *compacting* tracing: survivors are
copied so the live objects end up contiguous. That is what makes allocation a
pointer bump rather than a free-list search, and it is what makes object
addresses unstable — hence `fixed`, `GCHandle`, and the whole pinning story.

## The generational hypothesis, and the evidence for it

The generational design rests on a claim: most objects die young. It is not a
theoretical claim, it was measured, repeatedly, across languages, from the
early Lisp and Smalltalk collectors onward. Typical server workloads confirm
it brutally: the vast majority of a request's allocations are dead by the time
the response is written.

If most objects die young, then a collector that examines only the young
objects reclaims most of the garbage for a fraction of the work. That is gen0.
The complication is that an old object can hold a reference to a young one —
a cache entry pointing at a freshly parsed value — so tracing only gen0 could
collect something that is genuinely reachable.

The runtime solves this with **write barriers** and a **card table**. Every
reference-typed field assignment compiles to a store plus a tiny barrier that
marks a "card" — a small region of the heap — as dirty. When gen0 is collected,
the collector scans dirty cards in the older generations for references into
gen0 and treats them as roots. You pay a few instructions on every reference
store, forever, so that gen0 collections can stay short. That is the actual
price of the generational design, and it is one of the reasons writing to a
reference field is measurably more expensive than writing to an `int` field.

## What a collection does, in order

1. **Suspend.** Managed threads are brought to a safe point. This is
   cooperative, not preemptive — the JIT emits polls, which is why a tight loop
   with no allocation and no calls used to be able to delay a collection.
2. **Mark.** From the roots — statics, each thread's stack and registers, GC
   handles, the finalization queue — trace reachable objects and set a bit.
3. **Plan and relocate.** Decide new addresses for survivors, compacting away
   the gaps.
4. **Update references.** Every reference pointing at a moved object is
   rewritten. This is why pinned objects hurt: they cannot move, so the plan
   has to work around them.
5. **Resume**, and reset gen0's allocation pointer to the start.

Background gen2 collection overlaps most of steps 2-4 with your running
threads, using short suspensions rather than one long one. That is why the
number of collections is a poor proxy for pause time, and why
`GC.GetGCMemoryInfo().PauseDurations` is the honest metric.

## Numbers worth carrying

These are order-of-magnitude figures for 64-bit .NET 8 on a typical x64
server. They vary; the ratios do not.

- Object header plus method table pointer: **16 bytes** on every reference
  type instance. An "empty" class costs 24 bytes after alignment.
- A boxed `int`: **24 bytes**. A boxed `long`: 24. A boxed `Guid`: 32.
- An array adds a **length field**: `new byte[n]` costs roughly `24 + n`,
  rounded up to 8.
- The LOH threshold: **85,000 bytes**, configurable via
  `GCLOHThreshold` but almost never worth changing.
- A gen0 collection: typically **tens of microseconds** to a few hundred.
- A blocking gen2 collection on a multi-gigabyte heap: **tens to hundreds of
  milliseconds**. This is the thing your p99 is made of.
- `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread`: two reads and a subtraction,
  effectively free, safe to call inside a benchmark's setup.

## Where the cost actually shows up in a service

The failure mode that dominates real .NET services is not "too much garbage".
It is **promotion**. Something allocated per request survives long enough to
be copied into gen1 or gen2 — because it was held across an `await`, because it
went into a queue, because a closure captured it, because it was cached
briefly. Each survivor costs a copy plus a reference fix-up, and gen1's
survivors then cost again on promotion to gen2, where they must wait for the
rare and expensive full collection.

The diagnostic instinct that works: when gen0 counts are high but gen1 and
gen2 counts are near zero, the allocation rate is high and harmless — reduce
it if you want throughput, but it is not a latency problem. When gen1 and
especially gen2 counts climb, something is *surviving* that should not, and
the fix is a lifetime change, not a micro-optimisation. Chasing bytes when the
problem is lifetime is the most common wasted week in .NET performance work.

## Pooling, and its honest cost

`ArrayPool<T>` and `ObjectPool<T>` swap GC cost for bookkeeping and risk. The
buffer you rent is not zeroed unless you ask, so you can leak a previous
tenant's data. The buffer you return must genuinely not be referenced any
more, and the compiler cannot help you check that. And a pooled object that is
long lived is by definition a gen2 object holding references to whatever you
left in it.

The rule that survives contact with production: pool **large, uniform,
short-lived buffers on a hot path you have measured**. Do not pool small
objects — the allocator beats you — and do not pool because it feels
disciplined. `RecyclableMemoryStream` and the ASP.NET Core pipelines exist
because HTTP body buffers meet that description exactly, and most application
code does not.

## When not to care

Most code should allocate freely and be readable. The generational collector
exists precisely so that the temporary list, the LINQ chain and the interpolated
string are affordable. The point at which allocation becomes a design input is
narrow and identifiable: a loop that runs millions of times, a request path at
high RPS, a latency SLO with a tight p99, or a memory-constrained container. If
you are not in one of those, `Span<T>` gymnastics buys you nothing and costs
readability, and reviewers should say so.

The corollary is that you should be able to *tell* which situation you are in,
with a number. That is what this sector's exercises are for: not to make you
allocation-averse, but to make you allocation-literate, so that "this allocates
too much" becomes a claim with a measurement attached rather than a taste.

## A note on `GC.Collect()`

There is a reason it is on every "code smell" list. Forcing a collection is a
blocking, full-heap operation that also resets the tuning heuristics the
collector has built up about your workload; the next several collections are
worse than they would have been. The defensible uses are: a test that needs
deterministic finalization or weak-reference behaviour, a benchmark harness
between iterations, and a genuine phase change in a long-running process — an
import finished, a level unloaded, the process is about to idle. Everything
else is superstition, and it is usually covering for a lifetime bug that the
collection does not fix.

## Exercise 1 - measuring what a delegate allocates

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex1.cs`.

`AllocationProbe.BytesFor(Action work)` returns the number of bytes allocated
on the calling thread while `work` runs, using
`GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread()`. A delegate that allocates nothing
must report `0`.

`AllocationProbe.CompareBuilders(int count)` returns
`(long Naive, long Builder)`: the bytes allocated by joining the numbers
`0 .. count - 1` with `result += i.ToString()` in a loop, and the bytes
allocated by the same join through a `StringBuilder`. Both must produce the
same string; only the byte counts differ. `count` below zero throws
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.

```
CompareBuilders(200)   ->  Naive around 60,000, Builder under 2,000
CompareBuilders(0)     ->  both tiny, both non-negative
```

The gate asserts `Naive > Builder * 5` and that both joins produce
`"0123...199"`, not exact byte counts — those move between runtimes.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The probe is three lines and no cleverness: read the counter, run the
delegate, read it again, subtract. Do not call `GC.Collect()` first — this
counter is a monotonic total of bytes handed out, not a measure of live heap,
so a collection changes nothing about it.

## Hint 2

The measurement shape, applied to something else:

```csharp
long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
var list = new List<int>(capacity: 1024);
long allocated = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before;
```

Keep the work inside the delegate small enough that nothing else on the thread
allocates in between.

## Hint 3

`CompareBuilders` calls `BytesFor` twice, once per strategy, and returns a
tuple. Two details decide whether the numbers are honest: build the string
inside the delegate rather than outside it, and make sure the compiler cannot
discard the result — assign it to a field or a local you later read. Decide for
yourself whether `StringBuilder.Append` should take `i` or `i.ToString()`, then
measure both; the difference is the point of the exercise.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the string side first. Write the two join methods and convince
yourself they return the same text, then wrap them in measurement. If the
strings differ, the byte comparison is meaningless.

## Hint 2

`result += i.ToString()` is not one allocation. Expanded, it is
`result = string.Concat(result, i.ToString())`: a new string for the number,
plus a new string holding everything accumulated so far. That second one grows
every iteration, which is why the total is quadratic in `count`.

## Hint 3

For the guard, `ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegative(count)` is the
.NET 8 one-liner and it fills in the parameter name for you. For `count == 0`
both loops run zero times and both strings are empty — check your assertion
still holds when the numbers are near zero, and choose the comparison
accordingly.

## Exercise 2 - counting collections, cumulatively

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex2.cs`.

`CollectionWatch.Measure(Action work)` captures `GC.CollectionCount` for
generations 0, 1 and 2 either side of `work` and returns a
`CollectionDelta(int Gen0, int Gen1, int Gen2)` of the differences.

`CollectionDelta.IsConsistent()` returns whether the deltas obey the rule the
runtime guarantees: `Gen0 >= Gen1 >= Gen2`, and no member is negative.

`CollectionWatch.Describe(CollectionDelta delta)` renders the deltas for a log
line: `"gen0=3 gen1=1 gen2=0"`, or `"no collections"` when all three are zero.

```
Measure(() => { })                        -> usually (0, 0, 0)
Measure(() => GC.Collect())               -> Gen0 >= 1, Gen1 >= 1, Gen2 >= 1
new CollectionDelta(1, 2, 0).IsConsistent()  -> false
Describe(new CollectionDelta(0, 0, 0))       -> "no collections"
```

The gate forces one full collection and asserts each delta is at least 1 —
never an exact count, because the runtime is allowed to collect whenever it
likes.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read all three counters before the work and all three after, then subtract
pairwise. Reading them interleaved with the work — gen0 before, gen2 after the
first half — is how you produce a delta that violates the rule and then
disbelieve the rule.

## Hint 2

`GC.CollectionCount(n)` answers "how many collections of generation n or
higher have happened since the process started". So a single full collection
increments all three. A related shape:

```csharp
int before = GC.CollectionCount(2);
GC.Collect();
bool fullHappened = GC.CollectionCount(2) > before;   // true
```

## Hint 3

A `readonly record struct CollectionDelta(int Gen0, int Gen1, int Gen2)` gives
you equality and deconstruction for free, and `IsConsistent` is one boolean
expression over its members. For `Describe`, decide whether "no collections"
means all three deltas are zero or just gen0 — given the cumulative rule, those
two definitions are the same, and being able to say why is the exercise.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the assertion you want to be able to make in a log: "this request
caused two gen0 collections and no promotion". Which counters do you need, and
what would make that sentence a lie?

## Hint 2

Counts are not pause time. Two gen0 collections at 40 microseconds each are
invisible; one gen2 collection is the spike in your p99. If you want the
latency answer rather than the frequency answer, the API is:

```csharp
GCMemoryInfo info = GC.GetGCMemoryInfo();
TimeSpan lastPause = info.PauseDurations.Length > 0 ? info.PauseDurations[0] : TimeSpan.Zero;
```

## Hint 3

`Measure` must not itself allocate meaningfully before the second read, or you
risk causing the very collection you are counting. Capture the three "after"
values into locals immediately, then build the record from them — the order
matters more than it looks.

## Exercise 3 - a cache that lets go

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex3.cs`.

`WeakCache<TKey, TValue>` (where `TKey : notnull` and `TValue : class`) stores
`WeakReference<TValue>` values:

- `Set(TKey key, TValue value)` — adds or replaces.
- `bool TryGet(TKey key, out TValue? value)` — false when the key is absent
  **and** false when the target has been collected; in both cases `value` is
  null.
- `int Trim()` — removes every entry whose target is gone and returns how many
  it removed.
- `int Count` — entries currently stored, live or dead.

```
var cache = new WeakCache<string, byte[]>();
var payload = new byte[16];
cache.Set("a", payload);
cache.TryGet("a", out var got);   // true, got is payload
cache.TryGet("b", out _);         // false

// after the only strong reference is dropped and a collection is forced:
cache.TryGet("a", out _);         // false
cache.Count                       // still 1 - the dead entry is still there
cache.Trim()                      // 1
cache.Count                       // 0
```

The gate creates values inside a non-inlined helper method, drops the
reference, calls `GC.Collect()` and `GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers()`, then
checks the cache admits the value is gone.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `WeakReference<T>` is not a root, so the value can die while your dictionary
entry lives on. That asymmetry is the whole exercise: `TryGet` must handle a
*present entry with a dead target*, and `Trim` exists because nothing else
will ever remove that entry.

## Hint 2

The only correct way to read one:

```csharp
if (reference.TryGetTarget(out Movie? movie))
{
    // movie is a strong reference now; it cannot be collected while you hold it
}
```

`TryGetTarget` takes the strong reference atomically. An `IsAlive` check
followed by a separate read is a race you can lose.

## Hint 3

`Trim` cannot remove entries while enumerating the dictionary — that throws.
Collect the doomed keys into a list first, then remove them, and return the
count. One decision left to you: should `Set` on an existing key replace the
`WeakReference` object or reuse it via `SetTarget`? Both work; say why you
picked yours.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what a weak cache is *for*. It is for values that are expensive to
build but cheap to rebuild, where holding them forever would be worse than
occasionally missing. If a miss is catastrophic, this is the wrong structure —
which is the design point hiding inside the API.

## Hint 2

`out TValue? value` needs the nullable annotations to line up. Declaring the
method as `public bool TryGet(TKey key, [MaybeNullWhen(false)] out TValue
value)` is the BCL's own convention and lets a caller use `value` without a
null check after a `true`, exactly like `Dictionary.TryGetValue`.

## Hint 3

To see a value actually collected in a test, the value must not be reachable
from a stack slot the JIT still considers live. That is why the gate allocates
it inside a `[MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.NoInlining)]` helper and returns
only the key. If you write your own scratch test and it never reports a
collection, that — not your cache — is usually the reason.

## Exercise 4 - the 85,000-byte cliff

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex4.cs`.

Model the 64-bit managed size of a single-dimension array exactly as the
runtime lays it out: **24 bytes of overhead** (object header word, method table
pointer, length field plus its padding) plus the payload, with the total
rounded up to the next multiple of **8**.

- `HeapPlanner.ArrayBytes(int elementSize, int length)` — the size in bytes.
  `elementSize` below 1 and `length` below 0 both throw
  `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
- `HeapPlanner.LohThreshold` — the constant `85_000`.
- `HeapPlanner.Destination(int elementSize, int length)` — `"LOH"` when the
  size is at or above the threshold, otherwise `"Gen0"`.
- `HeapPlanner.MaxElementsInGen0(int elementSize)` — the largest `length`
  whose array still lands in gen0.

```
ArrayBytes(1, 0)            -> 24
ArrayBytes(4, 10)           -> 64
ArrayBytes(1, 1)            -> 32        (24 + 1, rounded up to 8)
ArrayBytes(4, 21242)        -> 84992     -> Destination "Gen0"
ArrayBytes(4, 21243)        -> 85000     -> Destination "LOH"
MaxElementsInGen0(4)        -> 21242
MaxElementsInGen0(1)        -> 84968
MaxElementsInGen0(85_000)   -> 0
```

Use `long` arithmetic internally: `ArrayBytes(8, int.MaxValue)` must not
overflow into a negative number.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two separate ideas are being tested and it helps to write them separately.
One is the layout arithmetic — overhead, payload, alignment. The other is that
the threshold applies to the *whole allocation*, header included, which is why
a payload of exactly 84,992 bytes can still be a large object.

## Hint 2

Rounding up to the next multiple of eight, without a loop and without floating
point:

```csharp
static long RoundUpTo8(long value) => (value + 7) & ~7L;
```

The mask trick works because 8 is a power of two. `(value + 7) / 8 * 8` is the
same thing if you prefer to read it.

## Hint 3

`MaxElementsInGen0` is the inverse of `ArrayBytes`. Solve it directly rather
than looping: the largest total that still counts as gen0 is `LohThreshold - 8`
once you account for alignment, so subtract the overhead and divide by the
element size. Then decide what to do when the answer would be negative —
`MaxElementsInGen0(85_000)` has to return something sensible, and a negative
length is not it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Work backwards from a question you would actually be asked: "how big can my
buffer be before it goes on the large object heap?" Every method here is one
phrasing of that question, and the arithmetic is shared.

## Hint 2

Check your model against a fact you can verify: an empty `object` costs 24
bytes on 64-bit (16 of header plus 8 of padding), and `new byte[0]` costs 24
too — header, method table pointer, and the length field. Every element you add
is pure payload from there.

## Hint 3

For the inverse, be careful with the boundary. Test your answer by feeding it
straight back in: `Destination(size, MaxElementsInGen0(size))` must be
`"Gen0"`, and `Destination(size, MaxElementsInGen0(size) + 1)` must be `"LOH"`.
If both hold for element sizes 1, 4, 8 and 16 you have it; if one fails you are
off by an alignment step.

## Exercise 5 - the allocation you did not write

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex5.cs`.

Three summing routines over the same numbers, and one measurement.

- `Totals.SumBoxed(IEnumerable<object> values)` — casts each element back to
  `int` and adds. Every element arrived boxed.
- `Totals.SumGeneric<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T>` — adds
  without boxing anything.
- `Totals.BoxAll(IReadOnlyList<int> values)` — returns `object[]`, the boxing
  step, so the gate can hand the same numbers to both paths.
- `Totals.CompareCost(int count)` — builds `0 .. count - 1`, then returns
  `(long Boxed, long Generic)`: the bytes allocated by boxing-then-summing and
  the bytes allocated by summing the `int` values directly.

```
SumBoxed(new object[] { 1, 2, 3 })   -> 6
SumGeneric(new[] { 1, 2, 3 })        -> 6
SumGeneric(new[] { 1.5, 2.5 })       -> 4.0
CompareCost(10_000)                  -> Boxed around 240,000+, Generic near 0
```

The gate asserts `Boxed > Generic * 10` and that both totals agree.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A boxed `int` on 64-bit costs 24 bytes: header word, method table pointer,
four bytes of payload, four of padding. Ten thousand of them is a quarter of a
megabyte of garbage that never appears in your source as a `new`.

## Hint 2

Generic math is the constraint that makes the second version allocation-free:

```csharp
static T Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : INumber<T> => a > b ? a : b;
```

`INumber<T>` (System.Numerics, .NET 7+) brings `T.Zero`, `T.One` and the
operators with it, so `total += v` compiles to an add for each value type the
JIT specialises.

## Hint 3

`SumGeneric` starts from `T.Zero` and accumulates with `+=`. The subtle part
is what you must *not* do: taking `IEnumerable<IComparable>` or calling
`v.CompareTo(other)` through an interface-typed local puts the boxing straight
back. Keep every operation on the constrained type parameter, and decide
whether your `CompareCost` should include the cost of building the source list
in both measurements or neither.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask where a value type has to live in order to be reachable through an
`object` reference. It cannot live on the stack — the reference would dangle.
So the runtime copies it onto the heap and hands you a pointer to the copy.
That copy is the box, and every cast back is a copy in the other direction.

## Hint 2

Boxing hides in more places than `object`. All of these box a value type:

```csharp
object o = 42;                          // the obvious one
IComparable c = 42;                     // interface-typed variable
ArrayList list = new(); list.Add(42);   // the pre-generics API
string s = string.Format("{0}", 42);    // params object[]
```

`Console.WriteLine($"{x}")` does not, because interpolated string handlers take
the value generically.

## Hint 3

If your generic version still allocates, the enumerator is usually the culprit
rather than the arithmetic: `IEnumerable<T>` forces an interface-dispatched
enumerator object. Measuring an array or a `List<T>` through its concrete type
gives the struct enumerator and near-zero bytes — worth trying both and noticing
the difference, since that is exactly the trade the BCL made.

## Exercise 6 - renting instead of allocating

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex6.cs`.

`ChunkCopier.CopyThrough(byte[] source, byte[] destination, int chunkSize)`
copies `source` into `destination` one chunk at a time, staging each chunk in a
buffer rented from `ArrayPool<byte>.Shared`, and returns the number of chunks
it used.

Rules the gate checks:

- The rented buffer is returned exactly once, in a `finally`, even when the
  copy throws.
- The payload length is `chunkSize` (or whatever is left), never
  `buffer.Length` — the pool hands back an array of *at least* the requested
  size.
- `destination` shorter than `source` throws `ArgumentException`;
  `chunkSize` below 1 throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
- An empty source copies nothing and returns `0`.

`ChunkCopier.RentedLengthAtLeast(int requested)` returns the actual length of
an array rented for `requested` elements (rent, read `Length`, return) — proof
that "at least" is not "exactly".

```
CopyThrough(new byte[10], new byte[10], 4)   -> 3   (4 + 4 + 2)
CopyThrough(new byte[0], new byte[0], 4)     -> 0
RentedLengthAtLeast(100)                     -> >= 100, usually 128
```

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The pool is a lending library with two rules that are not in the method name:
what you get back may be bigger than you asked for, and it contains whatever
the last borrower left in it. Every bug in pooled code comes from forgetting
one of those.

## Hint 2

The frame, applied to a different job:

```csharp
char[] buffer = ArrayPool<char>.Shared.Rent(needed);
try
{
    text.CopyTo(0, buffer, 0, needed);
    return new string(buffer, 0, needed);   // 0..needed, not 0..buffer.Length
}
finally
{
    ArrayPool<char>.Shared.Return(buffer);
}
```

## Hint 3

Rent once outside the loop, not once per chunk — the point is to allocate a
buffer zero times, and renting per iteration is only marginally better than
allocating per iteration. Each pass computes `taken = Math.Min(chunkSize,
source.Length - offset)`, copies `taken` bytes in and `taken` bytes out, and
advances. Decide for yourself whether `Return` should pass
`clearArray: true`, and be able to defend the answer in terms of what the
buffer held.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Before writing the pooled version, write the version that allocates
`new byte[chunkSize]` inside the loop and measure it with the probe from ex1.
The number you are trying to drive to zero is the reason for all the extra
ceremony.

## Hint 2

Spans make the copying readable and bounds-checked in one step:

```csharp
source.AsSpan(offset, taken).CopyTo(buffer);
buffer.AsSpan(0, taken).CopyTo(destination.AsSpan(offset));
```

`CopyTo` throws if the destination is too short, which is a better failure than
a silent partial copy.

## Hint 3

For the guards, decide the order: check `chunkSize` before touching the arrays,
and check the destination length before renting anything. A guard that throws
*after* the rent but *before* the `try` leaks the buffer for the lifetime of
the pool — that is the subtle one, and it is why the rent should be the first
statement before the `try` and nothing else should sit between them.

## Exercise 7 - the most expensive keyword in a type declaration

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex7.cs`.

`TrackedHandle` pretends to own an unmanaged handle. It writes what happened
into a shared `ConcurrentQueue<string>` so the gate can watch the sequence.

- The constructor takes the log and a name.
- `Dispose()` records `"dispose:{name}"`, releases the handle, suppresses the
  finalizer, and is safe to call twice (the second call records nothing).
- The finalizer records `"finalize:{name}"` and releases the handle.
- `Release` is the shared cleanup: `Dispose(bool disposing)` in the
  conventional pattern, where `disposing` is true only from `Dispose()`.
- `TrackedHandle.IsClosed` reports whether the handle has been released.

Then `HandleLab.AbandonOne(ConcurrentQueue<string> log)` creates a
`TrackedHandle` named `"abandoned"` inside a non-inlined helper, drops it,
forces `GC.Collect()` and `GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers()`, and returns.

```
using (var h = new TrackedHandle(log, "used")) { }
// log: "dispose:used"          - and no "finalize:used", ever

HandleLab.AbandonOne(log);
// log contains "finalize:abandoned"
```

The gate asserts that a disposed handle never produces a `finalize` entry and
that an abandoned one does.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex7
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the cost, not the code. A type with a finalizer is put on the
finalization queue when it is allocated, so the collector cannot reclaim it in
the pass that first notices it is unreachable — the finalizer thread has to run
first, which means at least one extra generation of survival for every
instance. `SuppressFinalize` is how a disposed object buys its way out.

## Hint 2

Do not write a finalizer for a type that owns only managed objects. This is
the whole rule, and the modern version is stronger: own unmanaged resources
through a `SafeHandle` and write no finalizer at all, because `SafeHandle`
already has a correct one and is robust against being finalized halfway
through a P/Invoke.

## Hint 3

`AbandonOne` will not do what you expect unless the handle is genuinely
unreachable. Create it inside a helper marked
`[MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.NoInlining)]` that returns `void`, so no stack
slot in the caller keeps it alive; then collect, wait for finalizers, and
collect again — the first pass queues the finalizer, the wait runs it. Whether
you need that second collect for this exercise is worth thinking through.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - parsing without the garbage

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Ex8.cs`.

A settings line looks like `"host=db1;port=5432;mode=fast"`. Parse it with
spans.

- `SettingsReader.CountPairs(ReadOnlySpan<char> text)` — how many `key=value`
  pairs there are, allocating **nothing**. An empty span is `0`; empty
  segments (`"a=1;;b=2"`) are skipped; a segment with no `=` is skipped.
- `SettingsReader.FindValue(ReadOnlySpan<char> text, ReadOnlySpan<char> key)` —
  returns the value as a `string`, or `null` when the key is absent. Exactly
  one string is allocated on a hit and none on a miss. Keys are compared
  ordinally, case sensitively. The first match wins.
- `SettingsReader.TryFindValue(ReadOnlySpan<char> text, ReadOnlySpan<char>
  key, out ReadOnlySpan<char> value)` — the zero-allocation form the other two
  build on.

```
CountPairs("host=db1;port=5432")        -> 2
CountPairs("a=1;;b=2;oops")             -> 2
FindValue("host=db1;port=5432", "port") -> "5432"
FindValue("host=db1", "user")           -> null
FindValue("k=", "k")                    -> ""
```

The gate measures allocations: `CountPairs` and a miss must allocate zero
bytes, and a hit must allocate no more than the value string itself.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`text.Split(';')` is the instinct and it is the thing being trained out of
you: it allocates an array plus a string per segment before you have decided
whether you need any of them. Everything here is `IndexOf` plus `Slice` on the
span you were handed.

## Hint 2

The walk, in the shape you want:

```csharp
while (!remaining.IsEmpty)
{
    int end = remaining.IndexOf(';');
    ReadOnlySpan<char> segment = end < 0 ? remaining : remaining[..end];
    remaining = end < 0 ? default : remaining[(end + 1)..];
    // ... look at segment ...
}
```

`ReadOnlySpan<char>` supports range syntax, and `remaining[..end]` copies
nothing — it is a new view over the same characters.

## Hint 3

Write `TryFindValue` first and let the other two lean on it: `FindValue` is
`TryFindValue(...) ? value.ToString() : null`, and `ToString()` on a span is
the one allocation the contract allows. The decision left to you is what
`SequenceEqual` versus `Equals(..., StringComparison.Ordinal)` buys you for
the key comparison — one of them is doing exactly what you asked and the other
is doing slightly more.

## Hint 1

A `ReadOnlySpan<char>` over a string is a reference plus a length. Slicing it
changes the two numbers and touches no memory, which is why the whole parse
can be free. The cost only appears when you materialise something the caller
can keep — a `string`, an array, a list.

## Hint 2

Spans are `ref struct`s and that constrains the code you can write around
them. All of these are compile errors, on purpose:

```csharp
class C { ReadOnlySpan<char> field; }              // no: may not be a field
async Task M(ReadOnlySpan<char> s) { await ...; }  // no: may not cross an await
var f = () => span.Length;                          // no: may not be captured
```

Because a span may point at stack memory, the compiler refuses to let it
outlive its frame.

## Hint 3

The empty and malformed cases are where the marks are. Decide what
`"a=1;;b=2"` means (an empty segment, skipped), what `"oops"` means (no `=`,
skipped), and what `"k="` means (present with an empty value, which is *not*
the same as absent). Write those three down before you write the loop, and the
loop writes itself.

## Challenge - a batch under budget

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Challenge.cs`. Three ideas from this
sector meet: a rented buffer, span parsing, and a measurement that keeps you
honest.

A batch is one string of records separated by `'\n'`, each record
`"id=<id>;qty=<n>"`:

```
id=a41;qty=5
id=b02;qty=12
id=c19;qty=3
```

Implement:

- `BatchProcessor.Process(ReadOnlySpan<char> batch, Span<char> scratch, out
  int written)` — walks the batch, sums the quantities, writes a normalised
  summary of the form `"a41:5;b02:12;c19:3"` into `scratch`, sets `written` to
  the number of characters used, and returns the total quantity. It allocates
  **nothing**. A record missing either field, or with a quantity that is not a
  non-negative integer, is skipped. If `scratch` is too small it throws
  `ArgumentException` before writing anything partial.
- `BatchProcessor.Run(string batch)` — rents a `char[]` from
  `ArrayPool<char>.Shared` big enough for any summary the batch can produce,
  calls `Process`, and returns
  `BatchReport(int Processed, long TotalQuantity, string Summary, long
  AllocatedBytes, int Gen0Collections)`. `AllocatedBytes` is what the run cost
  on this thread and `Gen0Collections` is the gen0 delta across it.
- `BatchProcessor.RunNaive(string batch)` — the same result computed the
  obvious way: `Split('\n')`, `Split(';')`, `Split('=')`, a `List<string>` and
  `string.Join`. Same `BatchReport` shape.

```
Run("id=a41;qty=5\nid=b02;qty=12")
  -> Processed 2, TotalQuantity 17, Summary "a41:5;b02:12"
Run("id=a41;qty=5\nbroken\nid=c19;qty=x")
  -> Processed 1, TotalQuantity 5, Summary "a41:5"
Run("")   -> Processed 0, TotalQuantity 0, Summary ""
```

Honest difficulty note: the parsing is the easy half. The hard half is
sizing the scratch buffer without allocating to find out, and keeping `Run`'s
own bookkeeping out of the measurement. The gate asserts both implementations
agree on `Processed`, `TotalQuantity` and `Summary`, and that
`Run(...).AllocatedBytes` is at most a third of `RunNaive(...).AllocatedBytes`
on a hundred-record batch.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Do the sizing arithmetic on paper. Every record contributes at most its own
characters to the summary, and the separators only ever get shorter (`;qty=`
becomes `:`), so the batch's own length is a safe upper bound for the scratch
buffer. That is the trick: you never need to count first, because a bound you
can prove is as good as an exact size.

## Hint 2

Writing into a span without a `StringBuilder`:

```csharp
if (!source.TryCopyTo(destination[written..])) throw new ArgumentException(...);
written += source.Length;
destination[written++] = ';';
```

For the number, `qty.TryFormat(destination[written..], out int used)` writes
the digits straight into the buffer with no intermediate string.

## Hint 3

Structure `Run` as: rent, measure, release. Take the allocation and collection
counters immediately before the `Process` call and immediately after the single
`new string(buffer, 0, written)`, so the report covers the parse and its one
deliberate allocation and nothing else. The decision left to you is whether the
`BatchReport` construction itself falls inside the measured window — it is a
record, so it allocates, and being able to say how much your measurement costs
is part of measuring.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write `RunNaive` first and measure it. It is ten lines, it is obviously
correct, and it gives you both the expected answers and the number you have to
beat. Optimising before you have a baseline is how people ship faster code that
is wrong.

## Hint 2

Parse each record by finding the two field boundaries rather than splitting:

```csharp
ReadOnlySpan<char> record = ...;             // "id=a41;qty=5"
int semi = record.IndexOf(';');
ReadOnlySpan<char> first = record[..semi];   // "id=a41"
ReadOnlySpan<char> second = record[(semi + 1)..];
```

then check each field's prefix with `StartsWith("id=")` and slice past it.
`int.TryParse(span, out int qty)` accepts a span directly - no substring
needed.

## Hint 3

Skipping is where the two implementations drift apart. Decide precisely what
"skipped" means — not counted in `Processed`, not added to the total, and not
written to the summary — and make sure a skipped record leaves `written`
exactly where it was. The cheapest way to get that right is to build each
record's summary fragment only after both fields have validated.

## Review 1 - build the collector, then you will stop guessing

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC01_GcGenerations/Review1.cs`. Same ideas, opposite
direction: instead of measuring a collector, you implement one.

`GenerationalHeap(int gen0Budget, int gen1CollectionEvery)` models three
generations. Reachability is simplified to roots only — no object graph.

- `Allocate(string id, int bytes)` — puts a new object in gen0. If it would
  push gen0 past its budget, a gen0 collection runs **first**, then the object
  is allocated. Allocating an id that already exists throws
  `ArgumentException`.
- `Root(string id)` / `Unroot(string id)` — add or remove a strong root.
  Objects are allocated rooted.
- `Watch(string id)` — register a weak handle. A weak handle never keeps an
  object alive.
- `Collect(int generation)` — collects generations `0 .. generation`. Rooted
  objects in those generations survive and are promoted by one generation,
  capped at 2; unrooted ones are removed. Every collection adds the surviving
  bytes to `BytesCopied` — the cost model of a copying collector.
- Automatic escalation: every `gen1CollectionEvery`-th automatic gen0
  collection is a gen1 collection instead.
- `Gen0Bytes`, `Gen1Bytes`, `Gen2Bytes`, `Collections0`, `Collections1`,
  `Collections2`, `BytesCopied` — the counters.
- `int ClearDeadWatches()` — drops weak handles whose object is gone and
  returns how many. `bool IsAlive(string id)`.

```
var heap = new GenerationalHeap(gen0Budget: 100, gen1CollectionEvery: 3);
heap.Allocate("a", 40); heap.Allocate("b", 40);
heap.Unroot("b");
heap.Allocate("c", 40);          // 120 > 100, so a gen0 collection runs first
heap.Collections0                // 1
heap.IsAlive("b")                // false - unrooted when the collection ran
heap.Gen1Bytes                   // 40 - "a" survived and was promoted
heap.Gen0Bytes                   // 40 - "c", allocated after the collection
heap.BytesCopied                 // 40
```

Then answer the weak-reference question in code:
`GenerationalHeap.SurvivesWith(bool rooted, bool watched)` returns whether an
object with those two properties survives a collection — the one-line summary
of what a `WeakReference` does and does not promise.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc01_gc_generations review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Model an object as a small record — id, bytes, generation, rooted — in a
dictionary keyed by id. Then a collection is one pass: partition the objects
in the collected generations into survivors and casualties, promote the
survivors, delete the casualties, add the survivors' bytes to `BytesCopied`.

## Hint 2

Promotion, capped:

```csharp
obj.Generation = Math.Min(obj.Generation + 1, 2);
```

and the generation totals are derived rather than stored: sum the bytes of
objects whose generation matches. Deriving them means one fewer thing to keep
in sync, and the sums are small.

## Hint 3

The ordering in `Allocate` is the part the gate probes hardest: check the
budget against the *current* gen0 bytes, collect if the new object would
exceed it, and only then add — so the new object never participates in the
collection that made room for it. That is what the real allocator does, and
getting it backwards makes brand-new objects mysteriously get promoted. You
decide whether a single object larger than the whole budget is an error or an
allocation that simply proceeds; say why.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Everything in this sector was one claim: a collection costs what survives.
Your `BytesCopied` counter is that claim made executable. Before you write the
class, predict what `BytesCopied` should be after a workload that allocates
ten megabytes of immediately-dead objects — the answer is zero, and your
implementation has to agree.

## Hint 2

Two counters that are easy to get wrong. `Collections0` counts collections of
generation 0 *or higher*, exactly like `GC.CollectionCount(0)` — so a gen1
collection increments both `Collections0` and `Collections1`. And the
escalation counter counts *automatic* collections triggered by allocation, not
explicit `Collect` calls.

## Hint 3

`SurvivesWith` is deliberately trivial to write and the point is what it says:
a weak handle contributes nothing to survival, so the answer depends on
`rooted` alone. Where the weak handle does matter is `ClearDeadWatches` — the
handle outlives its object and is the entry that leaks if nobody trims it,
which is exactly the bug ex3 was built around.

lessons.summary: Eight collections, one question: which one, and how do you know? lessons.briefing:
# V3·C2 — Collections: choosing between them with numbers

Every team has an argument about `List` versus `LinkedList`, and it is always
conducted in adjectives. "Insertion is O(1)." "Yes, but it is slow." Both
sides are right, which is how you know the argument is missing a number.

The previous sector gave you one of the numbers: bytes allocated. This one
gives you the rest. By the end you should be able to answer "which collection"
with an estimate — how many element moves, how many rehashes, how many
comparisons, how many cache lines — and be able to say what would change your
mind. That is a different skill from memorising a complexity table, and it is
the one that survives contact with a profiler.

## The table is true and insufficient

Asymptotic complexity tells you how a cost grows. It says nothing about the
constant, and for the sizes most code actually handles, the constant is the
whole story. `LinkedList<T>.AddAfter` really is O(1) and really is slower than
`List<T>.Insert` at n = 1,000, because the list's "expensive" operation is a
single `Array.Copy` of contiguous memory — which modern hardware does at tens of
gigabytes a second — while the linked list's "cheap" operation allocates a node
and follows a pointer into cold memory.

The rule to carry: **contiguity beats asymptotics until n is large or the
element is big.** A `List<T>` walk touches one cache line per few elements; a
`LinkedList<T>` walk touches one cache line per element, in whatever order the
allocator happened to place them.

```csharp
// O(n) and fast: one contiguous move of 4,000 bytes.
list.Insert(500, item);

// O(1) and slower: allocate a node, write three pointers, touch cold memory.
linked.AddAfter(node, item);
```

## Where a dictionary actually spends its time

`Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` is an array of buckets plus an array of entries.
A lookup hashes the key, maps the hash to a bucket, then walks a chain of
entries comparing hashes first and keys second. So a lookup costs: one hash
computation, one or two cache misses, and however many comparisons the chain
requires.

Three consequences you can act on:

- **Your `GetHashCode` is the performance.** A hash that collides turns the
  chain walk into a linear scan. XOR-ing two fields is the classic way to
  produce a hash where `(1, 2)` and `(2, 1)` collide.
- **Growth is not free.** The dictionary resizes when it fills, choosing the
  next prime capacity and rehashing every entry. n inserts into a default
  dictionary cost roughly 2n entry copies across the resizes. Passing a
  capacity avoids all of them.
- **String keys are compared, not just hashed.** `StringComparer.Ordinal` is
  measurably faster than the culture-aware default, and it is what you almost
  always meant.

## Exercise 1 - the cost table you can defend

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC02_CollectionsByNumbers/Ex1.cs`. Implement
`CostModel.ComplexityOf(string collection, string operation)` returning


## Exercise 7 - build once, read a million times

TValue>` builds a perfect-ish lookup once (sorted keys plus binary search) and

```

```

## Exercise 8 - the factory that runs twice

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC02_CollectionsByNumbers/Ex8.cs`.
`ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd` may invoke your factory more than once for the
same key under contention, and the loser's value is discarded — which is a
disaster if that value is a connection. Implement `CachedFactory.GetOrAdd` the
naive way and `CachedFactory.GetOrAddLazy` with `Lazy<T>`, and count factory
invocations under concurrent pressure.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc02_collections_by_numbers ex8
```

## Challenge

`WorkloadPlanner` takes a workload — element count, read/write mix, whether
order matters, whether keys are ranges — estimates the cost of three candidate
structures in comparable units, and returns both the recommendation and the
runner-up with the margin. Then you implement the structure it picks. A
recommendation you cannot compute is a preference.

## Review

`review1` is the LRU cache: a `Dictionary` for O(1) lookup and a doubly linked
list for O(1) recency, which is the one design where the linked list genuinely
earns its place — because you always hold the node, so you never walk. Get the
eviction order right and you have used every idea in this sector at once.
