# Reading - csharp/v3cc02_collections_by_numbers

## Notes

**Complexity is the growth rate; the constant is the experience.** For n in the
hundreds or low thousands — where most application collections live — a
contiguous O(n) operation routinely beats a pointer-chasing O(1) one. The
question to ask is not "which is asymptotically better" but "at my n, which
does fewer expensive things", where the expensive thing is usually a cache
miss, not an instruction.

**A cache line is 64 bytes.** That is eight `long`s, sixteen `int`s, or four
object references. A `List<int>` walk pulls sixteen elements per miss; a
`LinkedList<int>` walk pulls one node per miss and the node is 40 bytes of
which 4 are your data. This single fact explains most of the surprising
benchmark results in this area, including why `List<T>.Contains` beats
`HashSet<T>.Contains` for small n.

**Dictionary layout, precisely.** Two arrays: `int[] buckets` holding a 1-based
index into `Entry[] entries`, and the entries themselves holding
`{ int hashCode, int next, TKey key, TValue value }`. A lookup computes the
hash, indexes the bucket, then follows `next` comparing *stored hash codes*
first — an int comparison — and only calling `Equals` when the hashes match.
That is why a cheap `GetHashCode` matters more than a cheap `Equals`.

**Growth is doubling for `List`, next-prime for `Dictionary`.** `List<T>`
starts at 4 and doubles; `Dictionary` walks a table of primes (3, 7, 17, 37,
71, 163, 353, ...). Both give amortised O(1) append, and both make n insertions
copy roughly 2n elements in total if you do not pass a capacity. `EnsureCapacity`
exists on both and is the cheapest performance fix in .NET.

**`SortedList` and `SortedDictionary` are not variants of each other.**
`SortedList` is two parallel arrays: O(log n) lookup, O(n) insert, compact and
cache friendly, great for build-then-read. `SortedDictionary` is a red-black
tree: O(log n) insert and lookup, a node per element, better for churn. Picking
the wrong one is a factor-of-ten mistake in either direction depending on the
workload.

**Immutability has a price list.** `ImmutableList<T>` is a balanced tree —
O(log n) indexing, a node per element, and every "mutation" allocates the path.
`ImmutableArray<T>` is a plain array behind a struct wrapper — O(1) indexing,
and every mutation copies the whole thing. They are opposite trade-offs sharing
a name prefix, and the common error is choosing `ImmutableList` for a
read-mostly collection that should have been `ImmutableArray`.

**`FrozenDictionary` (`.NET 8`) is a build-once specialisation.** Creating one
is markedly more expensive than creating a `Dictionary`; reads are faster,
sometimes substantially so for string keys, because it analyses the key set at
build time and picks a strategy. It is for lookup tables built at startup and
read for the life of the process, and for nothing else.

## ex1

Really testing: whether your table has the exceptions in it. Anyone can recite
"dictionary lookup is O(1)". The differentiating answers are the awkward ones:
`List.Insert(0, x)` is O(n) because everything shifts; `List.Remove(x)` is O(n)
because it searches first; `Dictionary` enumeration order is undefined and must
not be relied on even though it looks insertion-ordered; `SortedList.Add` is
O(n) despite the O(log n) search, because the arrays shift. The classic mistake
is quoting the amortised figure without the word "amortised" and then being
surprised by a latency spike at a resize.

## ex2

Really testing: that O(1) is not a synonym for fast. The list's insert moves
`count - index` elements with one `Array.Copy`, which for 1,000 four-byte
elements is a single sub-microsecond memory move; the linked list allocates a
40-byte node, writes three references, and puts your next traversal on a cold
line. The classic mistake is reaching for `LinkedList<T>` after reading a
complexity table. The honest rule: `LinkedList<T>` earns its place only when
you already hold the node — so no traversal is needed to find it — which is
precisely the LRU cache in the review.

## ex3

Really testing: that a hash table is not always the answer. Binary search over
a sorted array costs `log2(n)` comparisons — 10 for a thousand elements, 20 for
a million — with perfect locality and zero per-element overhead, and it gives
you ordering, range queries and predictable memory for free. A dictionary costs
one hash plus one or two probes but adds ~24 bytes of overhead per entry and
loses ordering entirely. The classic mistake is a `Dictionary<int, T>` built
once from a dense key range where an array indexed by key would have been both
faster and simpler.

## ex4

Really testing: that `GetHashCode` is not a formality. XOR-ing fields makes
`(1, 2)` and `(2, 1)` collide, and any symmetric key set — coordinates, pairs,
from/to routes — degenerates to a linear scan. `HashCode.Combine` mixes with a
non-commutative function so order matters and bit patterns spread. The classic
mistake is a hash that is expensive rather than one that is bad: hashing a
whole string when a prefix would do is a cost on every single lookup, which is
usually worse than the occasional collision it prevents.

## ex5

Really testing: what capacity actually saves. n inserts without a capacity
means a sequence of resizes, each allocating a bigger pair of arrays and
rehashing every existing entry; the total entry copies are roughly 2n and the
total allocation is roughly twice the final size. Passing the capacity makes
all of it disappear. The classic mistake is passing the *byte* size or the
expected *maximum* rather than the expected count; the second is calling
`EnsureCapacity` inside the loop, which reintroduces the checks it was meant to
remove.

## ex6

Really testing: what "amortised" means, as arithmetic. Doubling means the
copies for n pushes are `1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/2 < n`, so fewer than one copy per
element on average, even though one unlucky push copies everything. The classic
mistake is growing by a constant — `capacity + 16` — which turns the total into
O(n²) copies and is a real bug people ship. The other point of the exercise is
the ring itself: `(head + 1) % capacity` is correct and a modulo; masking with
`capacity - 1` is correct only when the capacity is a power of two, which is why
`Queue<T>` grows the way it does.

## ex7

Really testing: that build cost is part of the choice. A structure that is 30%
faster to read but ten times more expensive to build is a win at a million
reads and a loss at ten. Computing the break-even point turns "frozen is
faster" into "frozen is faster above about 4,000 reads per build", which is a
sentence you can act on. The classic mistake is freezing a dictionary that is
rebuilt per request, where you pay the build cost every time and never reach
the break-even.

## ex8

Really testing: the `GetOrAdd` contract nobody reads. `ConcurrentDictionary`
does not hold a lock while your factory runs — deliberately, so a slow factory
cannot block the whole dictionary — so two threads can both miss, both run the
factory, and one result is silently discarded. If the factory opens a
connection, starts a timer or registers a handler, the discarded one leaks. The
fix is to store `Lazy<T>` values: the factory that creates the `Lazy` is
trivial and idempotent, and `Lazy<T>` with `ExecutionAndPublication` guarantees
the expensive work happens exactly once. The classic mistake is "assuming" the
dictionary locks, which is a bug you will never reproduce on your laptop.

## Further reading

- [List<T>](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.list-1) - capacity, growth, Insert and Remove costs.
- [Dictionary<TKey, TValue>](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.dictionary-2) - buckets, entries, capacity.
- [HashCode.Combine](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.hashcode.combine) - the mixing function you should be using.
- [FrozenDictionary<TKey, TValue>](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.frozen.frozendictionary-2) - build once, read forever.
- [ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.concurrent.concurrentdictionary-2.getoradd) - the factory-may-run-twice remark.
- [Choosing a collection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/collections/) - the BCL's own decision guidance.

# V3·C2 — Collections: choosing between them with numbers

## The question this sector answers

"Which collection should I use?" is asked constantly and answered badly,
because the usual answer is a complexity table and the usual reality is a
constant factor. This sector gives you a way to answer it with arithmetic you
can do in a code review: how many elements move, how many nodes allocate, how
many comparisons happen, how many cache lines get touched, and what the build
cost is versus the read cost.

## The structures, and what they really are

| Structure | Underneath | Strong at | Weak at |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `T[]` | contiguous memory | indexing, iteration | any resize |
| `List<T>` | array + count, doubles | append, index, iterate | insert/remove at front |
| `LinkedList<T>` | node per element | splice when you hold the node | anything requiring a walk |
| `Dictionary<K,V>` | bucket array + entry array | keyed lookup | ordering, memory per entry |
| `SortedList<K,V>` | two parallel arrays | build then read in order | insert into the middle |
| `SortedDictionary<K,V>` | red-black tree | ordered data with churn | locality, memory |
| `HashSet<T>` | dictionary without values | membership, set algebra | ordering |
| `Queue<T>` / `Stack<T>` | ring buffer / array | ends only | anything else |
| `ImmutableArray<T>` | array in a struct | read-mostly sharing | any mutation |
| `ImmutableList<T>` | balanced tree | persistent versions | indexing, allocation |
| `FrozenDictionary<K,V>` | analysed at build | read-only lookup tables | rebuilding often |
| `ConcurrentDictionary<K,V>` | striped locks + volatile reads | concurrent keyed access | atomic multi-key work |

## Worked example: the LinkedList argument, with numbers

```csharp
var list = new List<int>(Enumerable.Range(0, 1000));
list.Insert(500, 42);           // O(n): one Array.Copy of 500 ints = 2 KB
```

Two kilobytes of contiguous memory move at roughly 10 GB/s, so about 200
nanoseconds, most of it already in cache because you just walked there.

```csharp
var node = linked.First;
for (int i = 0; i < 500; i++) node = node!.Next;   // 500 cache misses
linked.AddAfter(node, 42);                          // then O(1)
```

Each `Next` is a dependent load — the address of the next node is not known
until the current one arrives — so the CPU cannot prefetch. Five hundred
dependent misses at ~80 nanoseconds each is 40 microseconds: two hundred times
slower, for the structure with the better complexity. The list only loses when
you already have the node and no walk is needed.

## Worked example: what a capacity saves

```csharp
var d = new Dictionary<int, int>();                 // capacity 0
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) d[i] = i;
// resizes at 3, 7, 17, 37, 71, 163, 353, 761, 1597
// entry copies: 3 + 7 + 17 + 37 + 71 + 163 + 353 + 761 = 1412

var d2 = new Dictionary<int, int>(1000);            // one allocation, zero rehashes
```

The same arithmetic applies to `List<T>` with doubling, and to
`StringBuilder`. If you know the count, say the count. It is the highest
value-per-character change available in .NET.

## Worked example: a hash that ruins a dictionary

```csharp
public override int GetHashCode() => Row ^ Column;            // (1,2) == (2,1)
public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(Row, Column);  // mixed
```

On a grid of coordinates the XOR version produces a triangular collision
pattern: every symmetric pair shares a bucket, chains grow, and lookups drift
from O(1) toward O(n). The symptom in production is a dictionary that is fine
in tests and quadratic in the field, because the test data was not symmetric.

## Worked example: the GetOrAdd trap

```csharp
// Wrong: the factory can run on several threads at once, and the losers'
// connections are dropped on the floor, unclosed.
var conn = cache.GetOrAdd(key, k => OpenConnection(k));

// Right: creating a Lazy is trivial and idempotent; opening happens once.
var lazy = cache.GetOrAdd(key, k => new Lazy<Connection>(
    () => OpenConnection(k), LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication));
var conn = lazy.Value;
```

`ConcurrentDictionary` does not hold a lock across your factory, on purpose.
The documentation says so in one sentence that almost nobody reads.

## Common mistakes

- Quoting amortised complexity as if it were worst case, then being surprised
  by the latency spike at a resize.
- `Dictionary` where an array indexed by a dense integer key would do.
- `ImmutableList<T>` for a read-mostly collection. You wanted
  `ImmutableArray<T>`; the list is a tree and indexing it is O(log n).
- `SortedDictionary` for build-then-read data. `SortedList` is two arrays and
  wins on locality and memory.
- Relying on `Dictionary` enumeration order. It looks insertion-ordered until a
  removal creates a free slot that the next insert reuses.
- `ContainsKey` followed by the indexer: two lookups where `TryGetValue` does
  one.
- `list.Any()` in a hot loop where `list.Count > 0` is free — `Any()` allocates
  an enumerator through the interface.
- Culture-sensitive string keys. `StringComparer.Ordinal` is faster and is
  almost always what you meant; the default comparer for `Dictionary<string,
  T>` is ordinal, but `Sort`, `Contains` on `List<string>` and
  `string.StartsWith` are not.

## Interview answer

*"How would you choose between a `List` and a `Dictionary`?"* — Say what the
access pattern is, then the numbers. If lookups are by key and n is more than
a few dozen, a dictionary; below that, a linear scan of a list is often faster
because it is contiguous and has no hashing. If the data is read far more than
written and needs ordering, a sorted array with binary search beats both on
memory and locality. Then name the deciding constraint: dictionary entries
carry per-entry overhead and lose ordering, so at very large n the memory
difference may decide it for you.

*"When would you use a `LinkedList<T>`?"* — When you already hold the node, so
no traversal is required — an LRU cache's recency list, or an intrusive queue
where each item knows its own node. Otherwise essentially never: the O(1)
splice is real, and finding the place to splice is O(n) with a cache miss per
step.

## Check yourself

1. `List<T>.Insert(0, x)` is O(n). Why is it still faster than a
   `LinkedList<T>` insert at 1,000 elements?
2. What two arrays make up a `Dictionary<K,V>`, and what does each entry hold?
3. Why does the dictionary compare stored hash codes before calling `Equals`?
4. n inserts into a default-constructed `Dictionary` cost roughly how many
   entry copies?
5. Why is XOR a bad way to combine fields into a hash code?
6. What is the difference between `SortedList` and `SortedDictionary`, and
   which one for build-once-read-often?
7. Why is `ImmutableArray<T>` O(1) to index and `ImmutableList<T>` O(log n)?
8. Under what circumstance does `ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd` call your
   factory twice, and what is the fix?
9. Growing a buffer by a constant amount instead of doubling changes the total
   copy cost from what to what?
10. When is `FrozenDictionary` the wrong choice?
11. How many cache lines does iterating a `List<int>` of 1,000 elements touch,
    approximately, and how many does a `LinkedList<int>` touch?
12. Why should you not rely on `Dictionary` enumeration order even though it
    usually looks insertion-ordered?
13. You need membership tests over 20 short strings, called in a hot loop.
    `HashSet<string>` or `string[]` with a linear scan — and how would you
    decide?
14. What does `EnsureCapacity` do that the constructor's capacity argument
    does not?

# Long reading - why the table lies, and what to use instead

## Big-O was designed for a machine that no longer exists

Asymptotic analysis assumes a uniform memory model: every access costs one
unit, wherever it lands. That was roughly true when the analysis was invented.
It has not been true since the mid-1990s. On a current server, an L1 hit is
about 1 nanosecond, an L2 hit 4, an L3 hit 15, and a trip to main memory 80 to
100 — a hundredfold spread that the notation cannot express and that dominates
most collection work.

So the practical model is not "count operations". It is **count memory
transactions, weighted by where they land**. `Array.Copy` of 4 KB is one
streaming operation the prefetcher understands perfectly. A walk over 1,000
linked nodes is 1,000 dependent loads the prefetcher cannot help with, because
each address is only known once the previous load returns. This is why the
"slow" O(n) operation routinely beats the "fast" O(1) one, and it is the single
most useful correction to the textbook you will make this year.

Asymptotics still matter — at n = 10 million, O(n²) is fatal regardless of
locality. The discipline is to know which regime you are in. Below a few
thousand elements, constants and layout decide; above a few hundred thousand,
growth rates decide; in between, measure.

## Inside `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`

The BCL implementation has been stable in shape for two decades and it repays
knowing.

```
buckets: int[]        // 1-based index into entries, 0 means empty
entries: Entry[]      // { int hashCode; int next; TKey key; TValue value; }
```

A lookup does: `hash = comparer.GetHashCode(key)`, `bucket = hash % size`,
then follow `entries[i].next` from `buckets[bucket] - 1`, comparing
`entries[i].hashCode == hash` before `comparer.Equals`. Two loads land on cold
memory in the common case — one in `buckets`, one in `entries` — which is why a
dictionary lookup is roughly the cost of two cache misses rather than the "one
operation" the table implies.

The details that fall out of this layout:

- The modulo is by a **prime**, which is why capacities are 3, 7, 17, 37, 71,
  163, 353, 761, 1597... A prime modulus spreads poorly-mixed hashes better
  than a power of two would. .NET Core added a fast modulo trick so the divide
  is no longer a stall.
- **Removal creates a free list.** Removed entry slots are chained into a free
  list and reused by the next insert, which is exactly why enumeration order
  stops resembling insertion order after any removal.
- **Hash codes are cached in the entry**, so a resize does not re-invoke your
  `GetHashCode`. It does re-bucket every entry, which is the O(n) part.
- For `string` keys, .NET uses a **randomised** hash seed per process and will
  switch a bucket to a collision-resistant comparer if a chain grows
  suspiciously long — a mitigation for hash-flooding denial of service. Two
  consequences: string hash codes are not stable across processes, so never
  persist them, and a dictionary under attack degrades rather than dying.

## Growth policies, and why doubling is the answer

Doubling gives amortised O(1) append because the total copy work for n
insertions is a geometric series that sums to less than n. Growing by a
constant `k` gives `n²/2k` total copies, which is a genuine O(n²) algorithm
hiding in something that looks like an append loop.

The BCL's choices: `List<T>` starts at 4 and doubles; `Queue<T>` doubles;
`Dictionary` moves to the next prime at least double the current;
`StringBuilder` chains 8,000-character chunks rather than copying, which is why
`StringBuilder` avoids the LOH and a growing `List<byte>` does not.

The growth factor is a memory-versus-copies trade. Doubling can waste up to
half the allocated space; some libraries use 1.5 to reduce that, at the cost of
more copies. .NET picked 2, and then gave you `EnsureCapacity` so you can opt
out of the guessing entirely.

## Set operations are not free

`HashSet<T>` gives you `UnionWith`, `IntersectWith`, `ExceptWith` and
`IsSubsetOf`, and their costs vary more than their names suggest.
`IntersectWith(other)` is O(n) when `other` is a `HashSet` with the same
comparer, because it can probe; when `other` is an arbitrary `IEnumerable` it
may materialise it first. `IsSubsetOf` on an `IEnumerable` counts distinct
elements, which allocates. The rule: when both sides are `HashSet<T>` **with
the same comparer**, the fast paths engage; otherwise, read the source or
measure.

The comparer detail matters more than it sounds. A `HashSet<string>` built with
`StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` and another built with the default comparer
are, as far as the fast paths are concerned, incompatible, and the operation
silently takes the slow route.

## Concurrency changes the shape of the question

`ConcurrentDictionary` is not "a dictionary that is safe". It is a different
data structure with different guarantees: lock striping for writes, lock-free
volatile reads, and — critically — **no atomicity across operations**.
`ContainsKey` followed by `TryAdd` is a race no matter how you squint.
`GetOrAdd` may run your factory more than once. `Count` takes every lock and is
O(number of locks). `ToArray` is a snapshot; enumeration is not — it is a
moving window that may or may not include concurrent writes.

The practical guidance that survives: use `ConcurrentDictionary` for a cache
whose values are cheap and idempotent to create, wrap expensive creation in
`Lazy<T>`, never build a compound invariant across two operations, and if you
find yourself needing one, you wanted a lock and a plain `Dictionary`.

## The immutable family

`ImmutableArray<T>` is a `struct` wrapping a `T[]`. Indexing is a bounds check
and a load; `Add` copies the whole array. It is the right choice for
configuration, lookup tables, and anything read far more than written.
Its default value is a struct with a null array, so an uninitialised
`ImmutableArray<T>` field throws on use — the one sharp edge.

`ImmutableList<T>` is an AVL tree. Indexing walks the tree, `Add` allocates
`log n` nodes on the path and shares the rest. It is the right choice when you
need many versions alive at once — an undo stack, a snapshot per request — and
the wrong choice for everything else, which is what most misuse looks like.

`FrozenDictionary` and `FrozenSet` (.NET 8) analyse the key set at creation and
select a specialised implementation — for example, comparing string lengths
first, or a single character at a discriminating position — and can be
several times faster to read than `Dictionary`. Creation is correspondingly
expensive. Break-even is typically in the thousands of lookups, which is
trivially met by a startup lookup table and never met by a per-request one.

## When not to think about any of this

The default should be `List<T>` and `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`, with a capacity
when you know the count. They are excellent, they are what every reader
expects, and swapping to something exotic costs comprehension. The moment to
reach for the analysis in this sector is when a collection is on a hot path
with a measured cost, when n is large enough that growth rate matters, or when
memory per entry has become a constraint. Choosing `FrozenDictionary` for a
five-element lookup because it is "faster" is the same error as choosing
`LinkedList` for insertion: a real property, applied where it cannot pay.

## Exercise 1 - the cost table you can defend

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC02_CollectionsByNumbers/Ex1.cs`.

`CostModel.ComplexityOf(string collection, string operation)` returns the
worst-case-or-amortised complexity as a string. Collections: `"List"`,
`"LinkedList"`, `"Dictionary"`, `"SortedList"`, `"SortedDictionary"`,
`"HashSet"`, `"Array"`. Operations: `"index"`, `"append"`, `"insertFront"`,
`"lookupByKey"`, `"containsValue"`, `"removeByKey"`, `"iterateInOrder"`.

Unknown collections or operations, and combinations that do not exist for that
collection (`"lookupByKey"` on a `List`), return `"unsupported"`. Comparison is
ordinal and case sensitive.

`CostModel.Explain(string collection, string operation)` returns one sentence
naming the *mechanism*, not the letter: for `("List", "insertFront")`,
`"every element shifts up one position"`.

```
ComplexityOf("List", "index")                   -> "O(1)"
ComplexityOf("List", "append")                  -> "O(1) amortised"
ComplexityOf("List", "insertFront")             -> "O(n)"
ComplexityOf("Dictionary", "lookupByKey")       -> "O(1)"
ComplexityOf("Dictionary", "iterateInOrder")    -> "unsupported"
ComplexityOf("SortedList", "append")            -> "O(n)"
ComplexityOf("SortedDictionary", "lookupByKey") -> "O(log n)"
ComplexityOf("LinkedList", "index")             -> "O(n)"
ComplexityOf("Array", "append")                 -> "unsupported"
Explain("List", "append")   -> "amortised because doubling makes the copies sum to less than n"
```

The gate asks for every pair. `"unsupported"` is a real answer, not a fallback
you can return for everything.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc02_collections_by_numbers ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is a lookup table, so build a lookup table: a
`Dictionary<(string, string), string>` keyed by the pair. A value tuple is a
perfectly good composite key and hashes correctly, unlike a concatenated
string, which inherits every delimiter bug you can imagine.

## Hint 2

The tricky rows are the ones where two operations share a name but not a cost:

```csharp
["SortedList", "lookupByKey"]  = "O(log n)"   // binary search over the key array
["SortedList", "append"]       = "O(n)"       // ...but the insert shifts both arrays
```

`SortedList` is the one people get wrong, because the search and the insert
have different complexities.

## Hint 3

Write the table, then read it back critically: `Array` has no `"append"`,
`Dictionary` has no `"iterateInOrder"`, and `List` has no `"lookupByKey"` or
`"removeByKey"` because it has no keys. Decide whether `"containsValue"` on a
`Dictionary` is `"O(n)"` or unsupported — it exists, it scans every value, and
saying so is the point.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Do not start from the letters. For each pair, describe in one sentence what the
machine does — "hashes, indexes a bucket, follows a short chain", "copies the
tail up one slot" — and the complexity falls out of the sentence. That is also
how you answer the question in an interview without sounding memorised.

## Hint 2

`"amortised"` is doing real work in this table and belongs on exactly the
operations that occasionally do O(n) work to buy cheap operations later:

```csharp
list.Add(x);   // usually a store; occasionally copies the whole backing array
```

An operation that is O(1) every single time — indexing an array — does not get
the word, and one that is O(n) every time does not either.

## Hint 3

For `Explain`, keep the sentences short and mechanical, and make sure the
`unsupported` pairs have an explanation too — "a Dictionary has no defined
order, so there is nothing to iterate in order" is more useful to a learner
than an empty string. Decide what `Explain` returns for a genuinely unknown
collection name, and be consistent with `ComplexityOf`.

## Exercise 2 - the argument, settled with a counter

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC02_CollectionsByNumbers/Ex2.cs`.

Insert `count` items into the middle of a collection of `initial` items, and
count what each structure actually does.

- `InsertionCost.ForList(int initial, int count)` returns
  `(int ElementMoves, int NodeAllocations, int PointerHops)`: a `List<T>`
  insert at index `k` moves `size - k` elements, allocates no nodes, and
  reaches the position by arithmetic (`0` hops).
- `InsertionCost.ForLinkedList(int initial, int count)` returns the same
  triple for a `LinkedList<T>`: no element moves, one node allocation per
  insert, and `k` pointer hops to walk to the position.
- Both insert at the middle, `k = size / 2`, recomputed as the collection
  grows.
- `InsertionCost.Recommend(int initial, int count)` returns `"List"` or
  `"LinkedList"` using this stated rule: a pointer hop costs 20 units (a
  dependent cache miss), a node allocation costs 8, and an element move costs
  1 (contiguous, prefetched). Ties go to `"List"`.

```
ForList(1000, 1)        -> (500, 0, 0)
ForLinkedList(1000, 1)  -> (0, 1, 500)
Recommend(1000, 1)      -> "List"      (500 vs 10,008)
Recommend(4, 100)       -> "List"
ForList(0, 3)           -> (0, 0, 0)   (middle of an empty list is index 0)
```

`initial` or `count` below zero throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc02_collections_by_numbers ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Nothing here needs a real collection — you are counting, not storing. Track the
current size in a local, and for each insertion work out `k = size / 2`, add
the costs, then increment the size. The gate can check exact numbers because
the model is arithmetic.

## Hint 2

The cost of a `List` insert, seen from the array's point of view:

```csharp
// Insert at k in a list of size n: elements k..n-1 move up one slot.
int moves = size - k;
```

Notice that inserting at the end costs zero moves and inserting at the front
costs `size` — the same method, a hundredfold difference, which is why
`insertFront` had its own row in ex1.

## Hint 3

`Recommend` is the weighted sum of the two triples, compared. The weights
encode the claim the sector is making — that a dependent cache miss is worth
about twenty contiguous element moves — so make them named constants rather
than magic numbers in an expression, and leave yourself able to change one and
see the recommendation flip. Try `Recommend(1_000_000, 1)` afterwards and see
whether it does.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Predict the answer before you write the code. For a thousand elements, the
list moves 500 ints — two kilobytes, one `Array.Copy`, sub-microsecond. The
linked list makes 500 dependent loads, each of which may miss cache. Which
number do you expect to dominate, and by roughly how much?

## Hint 2

The reason the walk is so expensive is that it cannot be pipelined:

```csharp
node = node.Next;   // the address of the next node is unknown
node = node.Next;   // until this load returns - no prefetching possible
```

A contiguous scan has the opposite property: the CPU can predict every address
and fetch ahead, which is why `moves` and `hops` deserve wildly different
weights.

## Hint 3

Watch the empty and tiny cases. `size / 2` of 0 is 0 and of 1 is 0, so the
first few inserts cost almost nothing in either structure; the divergence only
starts once the collection is big. Make sure `ForList(0, 3)` gives `(0, 0, 0)`
and convince yourself why — it is the sanity check that your `k` is recomputed
per insertion rather than fixed up front.

## Exercise 3 - hash lookup versus binary search

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC02_CollectionsByNumbers/Ex3.cs`.

`SortedIndex.Search(int[] sorted, int value, out int comparisons)` is a binary
search that follows the BCL convention: it returns the index of the match, or
the **bitwise complement** of the index where the value would be inserted.
`comparisons` reports how many elements it looked at.

`SortedIndex.InsertionPointOf(int[] sorted, int value)` turns a negative
result back into an index: `~result`.

`Lookup.Choose(int n, int reads, int writes, bool needsOrder)` returns
`"SortedArray"` or `"Dictionary"` by this rule, checked in order:

1. `needsOrder` is true -> `"SortedArray"` (a dictionary has no order to give).
2. `n <= 16` -> `"SortedArray"` (at that size the scan is contiguous and the
   hash is pure overhead).
3. `writes * 8 > reads` -> `"Dictionary"` (an insert into a sorted array
   shifts, so writes are the expensive side).
4. Otherwise `"SortedArray"`.

```
Search(new[] { 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 }, 7, out int c)   -> 3,  c == 2
Search(new[] { 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 }, 4, out c)       -> -3, c == 3
InsertionPointOf(new[] { 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 }, 4)    -> 2
Search(Array.Empty<int>(), 1, out c)            -> -1, c == 0
Choose(1000, 1000, 1, false)                    -> "SortedArray"
Choose(1000, 10, 100, false)                    -> "Dictionary"
Choose(1000, 1000, 1000, true)                  -> "SortedArray"
Choose(8, 1, 1000, false)                       -> "SortedArray"
```

Your search must be O(log n): a thousand-element array must never cost more
than 10 comparisons.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc02_collections_by_numbers ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The complement convention exists so one return value carries two answers:
"found, here" and "not found, but it belongs here". `~x` for a non-negative `x`
is always negative, so the sign is a free flag, and `~(-3 - 1)` gets you back —
or more simply, `~(~2) == 2`.

## Hint 2

The loop, with the overflow-safe midpoint:

```csharp
int low = 0, high = array.Length - 1;
while (low <= high)
{
    int mid = low + ((high - low) / 2);   // not (low + high) / 2
    ...
}
```

`(low + high) / 2` overflows for large arrays and is the textbook bug that
lived in the JDK for nine years.

## Hint 3

When the loop exits without a match, `low` is exactly the insertion point, so
`return ~low;`. Count a comparison each time you examine `array[mid]` — once per
iteration, not once per branch. The decision left to you is where to increment
the counter so that an empty array reports zero and a five-element search
reports at most three.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what each structure gives you beyond the lookup. A sorted array
answers "what is the next key after this one", "give me the range 100 to 200"
and "iterate in order" — none of which a dictionary can answer at all. That is
why `needsOrder` is the first rule and not a tie-breaker.

## Hint 2

The memory difference is worth having a number for. A `Dictionary<int, int>`
entry is 16 bytes plus a bucket slot, so about 20 bytes per element, versus 8
for two parallel arrays. At a million entries that is 20 MB against 8, and the
dictionary's are scattered while the arrays stream.

## Hint 3

Write `Choose` as an ordered sequence of early returns rather than one boolean
expression. The order is the specification: order beats size, size beats the
read/write mix. If you collapse it into a single condition you will get
`Choose(8, 1, 1000, false)` wrong, and that case is in the gate precisely
because it separates the two shapes.

## Exercise 4 - a bad hash, quantified

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC02_CollectionsByNumbers/Ex4.cs`.

`readonly record struct Cell(int Row, int Column)` is the key. Two comparers
implement `IEqualityComparer<Cell>`:

- `XorCellComparer` — `GetHashCode` is `Row ^ Column`.
- `MixedCellComparer` — `GetHashCode` is `HashCode.Combine(Row, Column)`.

Both `Equals` compare both fields.

`HashQuality.Measure(IEnumerable<Cell> keys, IEqualityComparer<Cell>
comparer, int buckets)` distributes the keys into `buckets` slots using
`(comparer.GetHashCode(key) & 0x7FFFFFFF) % buckets` and returns
`HashReport(int OccupiedBuckets, int LongestChain, double AverageProbe)`.
`AverageProbe` is the mean number of entries examined by a successful lookup,
which for a chain of length `L` is `(L + 1) / 2` per entry in it — round the
final average to three decimal places.

`HashQuality.SymmetricGrid(int size)` produces every `Cell(r, c)` for
`0 <= r < size` and `0 <= c < size`.

```
var grid = HashQuality.SymmetricGrid(16);            // 256 keys
HashQuality.Measure(grid, new XorCellComparer(), 512)
  -> OccupiedBuckets 16, LongestChain 16   (only 16 distinct hashes exist)
HashQuality.Measure(grid, new MixedCellComparer(), 512)
  -> OccupiedBuckets around 200, LongestChain 4 or so
HashQuality.Measure(Array.Empty<Cell>(), new MixedCellComparer(), 8)
  -> HashReport(0, 0, 0)
```

The gate asserts, over a 16x16 grid in 512 buckets, that the XOR comparer
occupies exactly 16 buckets with a longest chain of 16, that the mixed
comparer's longest chain is at most 8, and that both comparers agree on
equality for every pair.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc02_collections_by_numbers ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

XOR is commutative and self-inverse, and both properties hurt. `(1, 2)` and
`(2, 1)` produce the same hash, and `(3, 3)` and `(5, 5)` both produce zero. On
a square grid that collapses a two-dimensional key space into something close
to one dimension.

## Hint 2

Bucketing, with the sign handled:

```csharp
int bucket = (comparer.GetHashCode(key) & 0x7FFFFFFF) % buckets;
```

The mask clears the sign bit, because `%` on a negative int is negative in C#
and a negative bucket index is an exception waiting for the first key that
hashes high.

## Hint 3

Count into an `int[buckets]`, then derive everything from the counts:
occupied buckets are the non-zero ones, the longest chain is the maximum, and
the average probe is the sum over buckets of `L * (L + 1) / 2` divided by the
total number of keys. Decide what the report should say when there are no keys
at all — dividing by zero is not the answer the gate wants.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Equality and hashing are one contract with two halves, and only one half is
allowed to be approximate. Equal objects **must** have equal hash codes;
unequal objects may share one. Both comparers here are correct — neither is
buggy — which is the point: a legal hash can still destroy your performance.

## Hint 2

`HashCode.Combine` is not a convenience wrapper around XOR. It runs the
xxHash32 mixing steps, so each input is multiplied by a prime, rotated, and
folded into the accumulator in order:

```csharp
public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(Row, Column);
```

Order matters, bit patterns spread, and adjacent inputs land far apart.

## Hint 3

The average-probe figure is the one that connects this to a real dictionary. A
successful lookup in a chain of length L examines, on average, `(L + 1) / 2`
entries — so a perfect distribution gives 1.0 and every collision drags it up.
Compute it as a weighted mean over the chains, not as an average of averages;
those differ whenever the chains are uneven, which is exactly the case you are
measuring.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 - what a capacity argument buys

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC02_CollectionsByNumbers/Ex5.cs`.

Model the `Dictionary` growth policy: the first insert sizes the table to the
smallest prime in the table below that is at least 3, and every resize moves to
the smallest prime that is **at least double** the current capacity. When a
resize happens, every entry currently stored is rehashed into the new table —
that is the cost.

The prime table is supplied as `GrowthPlan.Primes` and starts
`3, 7, 11, 17, 23, 29, 37, 47, 59, 71, 89, 107, 131, 163, 197, 239, 293, 353,
431, 521, 631, 761, 919, 1103, 1327, 1597, 1931, 2333, 2801, 3371, 4049`.

- `GrowthPlan.NextPrimeAtLeast(int minimum)` — the first prime in the table at
  or above `minimum`; throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` if the table has
  nothing that large.
- `GrowthPlan.ForCount(int count)` — the capacities the table passes through
  while `count` items are inserted one at a time into a dictionary created with
  no capacity. `ForCount(0)` is empty.
- `GrowthPlan.EntryCopies(int count)` — the total entries rehashed across those
  resizes.
- `GrowthPlan.WithCapacity(int count)` — the single capacity a dictionary
  created as `new Dictionary(count)` uses.
- `GrowthPlan.SavedBy(int count)` — `(int Resizes, int EntryCopies)` avoided by
  passing the capacity.

```
ForCount(1)      -> [3]
ForCount(8)      -> [3, 7, 17]
ForCount(1000)   -> [3, 7, 17, 37, 89, 197, 431, 919, 1931]
EntryCopies(1000)-> 1700          (3+7+17+37+89+197+431+919)
WithCapacity(1000) -> 1103
SavedBy(1000)    -> (8, 1700)
EntryCopies(3)   -> 0             (three items fit the first table exactly)
```

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc02_collections_by_numbers ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Simulate the inserts rather than deriving a formula. Keep `capacity` and
`stored`; when `stored == capacity` and another item arrives, resize first —
which appends the new capacity to the list and adds `stored` to the copy
count — then store. The sequence falls out.

## Hint 2

The two "next prime" questions are different and both appear here:

```csharp
NextPrimeAtLeast(count);            // sizing to a known count
NextPrimeAtLeast(capacity * 2);     // growing an existing table
```

The first is why `new Dictionary(1000)` gives 1103 rather than 1000. The second
is why the sequence roughly doubles but never exactly.

## Hint 3

`EntryCopies` is the sum of the capacities *before* each resize, which is the
same as the sum of every capacity in the sequence except the last. Prove that
to yourself on `ForCount(8)` — the copies are 3 and 7, ten in total — before
writing the loop, and decide whether you compute it inside `ForCount` or as a
second pass over its result.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The result you are heading for is a sentence: "inserting a thousand entries
without a capacity rehashes 1,700 entries and allocates nine tables; passing
the capacity does neither." Get the sentence right and the code is a
transcription of it.

## Hint 2

The same arithmetic applies to `List<T>`, with doubling instead of primes:

```csharp
var list = new List<int>();          // 0, then 4, 8, 16, 32, ... 1024
var sized = new List<int>(1000);     // one array, no copies
```

For n items the total elements copied is just under n in both cases — the
geometric series — which is what "amortised O(1)" means as arithmetic rather
than as a slogan.

## Hint 3

Watch the boundary in `ForCount`. A dictionary resizes when it is *full and
another item arrives*, not when it reaches some load factor, so exactly three
items produce `[3]` and zero copies while four produce `[3, 7]` and three
copies. Getting that off by one shifts every later number, which is why the
gate checks the small cases as carefully as the thousand.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 - amortised, proved

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC02_CollectionsByNumbers/Ex6.cs`.

`RingDeque<T>` is a double-ended queue over a circular buffer.

- `RingDeque(int capacity = 4)` — capacity below 1 throws
  `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
- `PushBack(T item)`, `PushFront(T item)`, `T PopBack()`, `T PopFront()` —
  popping an empty deque throws `InvalidOperationException`.
- `Count`, `Capacity`, and `Copies` — the total number of elements ever moved
  by a growth, which is the amortisation evidence.
- Growing doubles the capacity and unrolls the ring so the elements are
  contiguous from index 0 again.
- `T this[int index]` — logical index from the front, `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`
  outside the range.
- `T[] ToArray()` — front to back.

```
var d = new RingDeque<int>(capacity: 2);
d.PushBack(1); d.PushBack(2); d.PushFront(0);   // grows here
d.ToArray()      -> [0, 1, 2]
d.Count          -> 3
d.Capacity       -> 4
d.Copies         -> 2
d.PopFront()     -> 0
d[0]             -> 1

var big = new RingDeque<int>(4);
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) big.PushBack(i);
big.Copies       -> 1020    ( 4 + 8 + 16 + ... + 512, strictly under 2 * 1000 )
```

The gate pushes a thousand items and asserts `Copies < 2 * 1000`, then
interleaves pushes and pops at both ends and checks the contents survive the
wrap.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc02_collections_by_numbers ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A ring is an array plus two numbers. Keep `head` (the index of the front
element) and `count`; the back is `(head + count) % Capacity`, and pushing to
the front is `head = (head - 1 + Capacity) % Capacity`. The `+ Capacity` is
there because C#'s `%` returns a negative result for a negative left operand.

## Hint 2

The logical-to-physical mapping is the same expression everywhere, so write it
once:

```csharp
private int PhysicalIndex(int logical) => (head + logical) % buffer.Length;
```

Then the indexer, `ToArray` and the growth all read the buffer through it and
none of them has to think about the wrap.

## Hint 3

Growth is the interesting method: allocate a buffer twice the size, copy the
elements in *logical* order into slots 0..count-1, set `head = 0`, and add
`count` to `Copies`. Doubling is what makes the copies sum to less than the
element count; try changing it to `capacity + 4` afterwards and watch `Copies`
go quadratic, which is the fastest way to feel what amortised means.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write `ToArray` and the indexer before the growth. If those two are right, the
growth is easy to verify — copy through them, so the new buffer is correct by
construction — and if they are wrong, every other bug you find will be a
symptom of them.

## Hint 2

`Queue<T>` in the BCL is exactly this structure, and its growth code contains
the same branch you will need:

```csharp
if (head < tail) Array.Copy(buffer, head, next, 0, count);
else { /* two segments: head..end, then 0..tail */ }
```

You can either write that branch or copy element by element through the
logical index. One is faster and one is obviously correct; at this size, pick
the obvious one and say why.

## Hint 3

The empty and full cases collide in a ring: `head == tail` means both. That is
why `count` is a field rather than something you derive from the two indices —
carrying the count is the standard fix, and it also gives you `Count` for free.
Decide what `PopBack` should leave in the vacated slot; for a reference type,
leaving the old value there keeps an object alive that the caller thinks they
have dropped.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - build once, read a million times

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC02_CollectionsByNumbers/Ex7.cs`.

`FrozenLookup<TKey, TValue>` where `TKey : IComparable<TKey>` is built once
from a sequence of pairs and never changes: sorted key and value arrays, binary
search on read, no buckets, no chains, no per-entry overhead.

- `static FrozenLookup<TKey, TValue> Build(IEnumerable<KeyValuePair<TKey,
  TValue>> pairs)` — sorts by key; a duplicate key throws `ArgumentException`
  naming the key.
- `bool TryGet(TKey key, out TValue? value)` and `int Count`.
- `IReadOnlyList<TKey> Keys` — in sorted order, which is the thing a
  `Dictionary` cannot offer.
- `IEnumerable<KeyValuePair<TKey, TValue>> Range(TKey inclusiveLow, TKey
  inclusiveHigh)` — the ordered-structure payoff: every pair whose key falls in
  the range, in order.

Then the economics:

`Economics.BreakEvenQueries(double buildCostUnits, double dictionaryReadUnits,
double frozenReadUnits)` returns the smallest whole number of reads at which
building the frozen structure has repaid itself, or `-1` when the frozen read
is not actually cheaper. Assume the dictionary's build cost is the baseline
and `buildCostUnits` is the *extra* cost of freezing.

```
var lookup = FrozenLookup<string, int>.Build(new Dictionary<string, int>
{
    ["delta"] = 4, ["alpha"] = 1, ["charlie"] = 3,
});
lookup.Keys                       -> ["alpha", "charlie", "delta"]
lookup.TryGet("charlie", out int v)  -> true, v == 3
lookup.Range("b", "d")            -> [charlie=3]
BreakEvenQueries(1200, 1.0, 0.7)  -> 4000
BreakEvenQueries(1200, 1.0, 1.0)  -> -1
BreakEvenQueries(0, 1.0, 0.7)     -> 0
```

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc02_collections_by_numbers ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two arrays, sorted together, is the whole structure. Sort the pairs once at
build time, split them into a `TKey[]` and a `TValue[]`, and every read is
`Array.BinarySearch` over the keys with the value taken from the same index.
The parallel arrays are what keep it cache friendly — one contiguous run of
keys, no per-entry object.

## Hint 2

`Array.BinarySearch` already returns the complement convention you implemented
in ex3, and that is exactly what `Range` needs:

```csharp
int start = Array.BinarySearch(keys, low);
if (start < 0) start = ~start;      // first key at or above low
```

so the range walk starts at the right place whether or not the boundary key
exists.

## Hint 3

`BreakEvenQueries` is one inequality: `build + n * frozen <= n * dictionary`.
Solve for `n`, round *up*, and handle the case where `frozen >= dictionary`
separately — no number of reads repays a structure that is not faster to read.
The decision left to you is what to return when the build is free and the read
is cheaper; zero and one are both defensible and only one matches the gate, so
reason it through rather than guessing.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what you are giving up. A frozen structure cannot be added to, so every
change means a rebuild. That is fine for a routing table loaded at startup and
absurd for a per-request cache — and the break-even calculation is how you turn
that instinct into a threshold you can quote.

## Hint 2

The duplicate-key check is easier after sorting, because duplicates are
adjacent:

```csharp
for (int i = 1; i < keys.Length; i++)
    if (keys[i].CompareTo(keys[i - 1]) == 0)
        throw new ArgumentException($"duplicate key '{keys[i]}'", nameof(pairs));
```

One pass, no set, no extra allocation — and it detects duplicates that
`Dictionary` construction would have thrown on anyway, at the same point in the
lifecycle.

## Hint 3

`Range` should be lazy or eager deliberately, not by accident. If you write it
with `yield return`, a caller who takes the first element does the minimum
work; if you build a list, the cost is paid up front but the result is stable
if the caller enumerates twice. Pick one, and be able to say which property you
chose.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - the factory that runs twice

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC02_CollectionsByNumbers/Ex8.cs`.

`ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, TValue>.GetOrAdd` does not hold a lock while your
factory runs. Under contention several threads can miss, all run the factory,
and all but one result is discarded — silently, without disposal.

`ExpensiveResource` counts its own construction and disposal:

- `ExpensiveResource(string key)` increments `ExpensiveResource.Created`.
- `Dispose()` increments `ExpensiveResource.Disposed`, is idempotent.
- `static void ResetCounters()`.

Implement:

- `CachedFactory.GetOrAddNaive(ConcurrentDictionary<string, ExpensiveResource>
  cache, string key)` — the direct `GetOrAdd` with a factory that constructs an
  `ExpensiveResource`.
- `CachedFactory.GetOrAddLazy(ConcurrentDictionary<string,
  Lazy<ExpensiveResource>> cache, string key)` — stores `Lazy<T>` with
  `LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication` and returns `.Value`.
- `CachedFactory.RaceNaive(int threads, string key)` and
  `CachedFactory.RaceLazy(int threads, string key)` — run `threads` parallel
  callers against one fresh cache and one key, and return
  `(int Created, int DistinctInstances)`.

```
RaceLazy(64, "db")   -> Created == 1, DistinctInstances == 1
RaceNaive(64, "db")  -> Created >= 1, DistinctInstances == 1
```

Note what the naive figures say: callers still all get the *same* instance —
the dictionary is not broken — but `Created` can exceed one, and every extra
instance was constructed, abandoned, and never disposed.

The gate runs the race repeatedly and asserts `RaceLazy` always reports
`Created == 1`, and that both always report one distinct instance.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc02_collections_by_numbers ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The dictionary's guarantee is about the *stored value*, not about your
factory. Exactly one value ends up in the dictionary and every caller receives
it; the factory is simply called optimistically by whoever gets there, as many
times as that happens.

## Hint 2

The fix works because the thing being raced becomes trivial:

```csharp
var lazy = cache.GetOrAdd(key, k => new Lazy<Resource>(
    () => new Resource(k), LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication));
return lazy.Value;      // the expensive work happens exactly once
```

Several `Lazy` wrappers may be constructed and discarded — they are cheap and
hold nothing — while `Lazy<T>` itself guarantees the expensive delegate runs
once.

## Hint 3

To make the race actually race, every caller has to be already running when
the starting gun fires: create dedicated `Thread`s that wait on a
`ManualResetEventSlim`, then `Set` it and `Join` them all. Do not use the
thread pool here — sixty-four pooled work items that all block would spend
seconds waiting for the pool to inject more threads. Count distinct instances
with a plain `HashSet<ExpensiveResource>`; the type does not override
`Equals`, so the default comparer is already reference equality. Whether
`RaceNaive` reports more than one creation on your machine is not guaranteed —
say what that tells you about the class of bug this is.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what the discarded value *was*. If it is an `int`, nobody notices. If it is
a database connection, a file handle, a timer or an event subscription, you
have leaked it: nothing disposes the loser, and nothing ever will. That is why
this is a correctness bug and not a performance note.

## Hint 2

The same shape appears elsewhere and is worth recognising:

```csharp
if (!cache.ContainsKey(key)) cache.TryAdd(key, Build(key));   // racy: two ops
cache.AddOrUpdate(key, Build, (k, old) => old);               // factory again
```

Any API taking a factory you do not control the timing of has this property.
`ConcurrentDictionary` documents it in one sentence; most callers have not read
it.

## Hint 3

`LazyThreadSafetyMode` has three values and only one is right here.
`PublicationOnly` allows several factory runs and keeps the first published
result — exactly the bug you are fixing. `None` is not thread safe at all.
`ExecutionAndPublication` locks around the factory so it runs once; note that
this means a slow factory blocks other threads asking for the same key, which
is the trade you are making and should be able to defend.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge - the recommendation you can compute

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC02_CollectionsByNumbers/Challenge.cs`.

A workload is
`Workload(int Elements, int Reads, int Writes, bool NeedsOrder, bool
NeedsRangeQueries, bool Concurrent)`. Three candidates: `"List"`,
`"Dictionary"`, `"SortedArray"`.

`WorkloadPlanner.Estimate(Workload workload, string candidate)` returns a cost
in units, or `double.PositiveInfinity` when the candidate cannot satisfy the
workload at all (no ordering from a `Dictionary`, no range queries from a
`Dictionary` or an unsorted `List`). The cost model, stated so the gate can
check it:

- `List` — a read is a linear scan: `Elements / 2.0` units. A write is an
  append: `1.0`.
- `Dictionary` — a read is `2.0` (hash plus two probes). A write is `3.0`.
- `SortedArray` — a read is `log2(Elements) + 1` units, rounded up to a whole
  comparison count. A write shifts half the array: `Elements / 2.0`.
- Total is `Reads * readUnits + Writes * writeUnits`.
- If `Concurrent` is true, `Dictionary` costs 1.4x (lock striping and volatile
  reads) and the other two are infinite, because they need external
  synchronisation that this model does not price.

`WorkloadPlanner.Recommend(Workload workload)` returns
`Recommendation(string Winner, string RunnerUp, double Margin)`, where
`Margin` is the runner-up's cost divided by the winner's, rounded to two
decimals, and `double.PositiveInfinity` when the runner-up cannot do the job.
Ties break in the order `Dictionary`, `SortedArray`, `List`.

Then implement `SortedArrayIndex<TValue>` — `Add`, `TryGet`, `RangeCount` — so
that the structure the planner recommends for an ordered, read-heavy workload
actually exists.

```
var readHeavy = new Workload(10_000, 1_000_000, 10, false, false, false);
Estimate(readHeavy, "Dictionary")     -> 2_000_030
Estimate(readHeavy, "SortedArray")    -> 15_050_000
Recommend(readHeavy).Winner           -> "Dictionary"

var ordered = new Workload(1_000, 10_000, 10, true, true, false);
Estimate(ordered, "Dictionary")       -> double.PositiveInfinity
Recommend(ordered).Winner             -> "SortedArray"
Recommend(ordered).Margin             -> double.PositiveInfinity
```

Honest difficulty note: the arithmetic is easy and the *ordering* of the
disqualifications is not. A candidate that cannot answer the question is
infinitely expensive, not merely expensive, and that has to be decided before
any multiplier is applied.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc02_collections_by_numbers challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Separate the two questions. First: can this candidate answer the workload at
all? That is a boolean about capabilities — ordering, range queries,
concurrency. Only if it passes do you compute a number. Mixing them produces a
`Dictionary` that scores well on a workload it cannot serve.

## Hint 2

The sorted array's read cost is comparisons, so it is logarithmic:

```csharp
double reads = Math.Ceiling(Math.Log2(Math.Max(elements, 1))) + 1;
```

The `Max` keeps `Log2(0)` — negative infinity — out of your model, and the
`+ 1` accounts for the final equality check. Ten thousand elements costs 15
units per read, which is why the read-heavy workload goes to the dictionary
despite the dictionary's higher write cost.

## Hint 3

`Recommend` sorts the three estimates and reports the top two. Because
infinities are involved, `double.PositiveInfinity / double.PositiveInfinity` is
`NaN` — so handle the "runner-up cannot do it" case explicitly rather than
letting the division produce something the gate cannot compare. The tie-break
order is given; implement it as a stable sort key rather than a chain of `if`s,
and you will not have to think about it again.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Every number in the cost model is a claim you could defend or attack. "A
dictionary read is two units" says a hash plus two cache misses; "a sorted
array write is Elements/2" says the shift dominates. Write them as named
constants with the claim in a comment, because the point of the exercise is
that a recommendation is only as good as the model behind it.

## Hint 2

Test the model against your intuition at the extremes before trusting it:

```
new Workload(10, 1000, 0, false, false, false)     // tiny, read-only
new Workload(1_000_000, 10, 1_000_000, false, false, false)  // huge, write-heavy
```

The first should favour the list — at ten elements a scan beats a hash — and
the second should favour the dictionary. If your model disagrees, either the
model or your intuition is wrong, and finding out which is the exercise.

## Hint 3

For `SortedArrayIndex`, `Add` must keep the array sorted, which is where the
`Elements / 2` write cost comes from — do the insertion with
`Array.BinarySearch` to find the position and `Array.Copy` to open the gap,
not by appending and re-sorting. `RangeCount` should be two binary searches and
a subtraction, not a walk; that is the whole reason the structure earned its
place on an ordered workload.

exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 - the one place a linked list earns its keep

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC02_CollectionsByNumbers/Review1.cs`.

`LruCache<TKey, TValue>` with a fixed capacity, every operation O(1):

- `LruCache(int capacity)` — capacity below 1 throws
  `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
- `bool TryGet(TKey key, out TValue? value)` — a hit moves the entry to the
  most-recent end; a miss changes nothing.
- `void Put(TKey key, TValue value)` — inserts or updates, marks the entry
  most-recent, and evicts the least-recently-used entry when the capacity is
  exceeded.
- `int Count`, `int Evictions`, `int Hits`, `int Misses`.
- `IReadOnlyList<TKey> KeysMostRecentFirst()` — for inspection.
- `TKey? LastEvictedKey`.

The internals are the point: a `Dictionary<TKey, LinkedListNode<Entry>>` for
lookup and a `LinkedList<Entry>` for recency. Because the dictionary hands you
the *node*, no traversal is ever needed — which is the one condition under
which a linked list beats an array.

```
var cache = new LruCache<string, int>(capacity: 2);
cache.Put("a", 1);
cache.Put("b", 2);
cache.TryGet("a", out _);        // true - "a" is now the most recent
cache.Put("c", 3);               // evicts "b", the least recently used
cache.KeysMostRecentFirst()      -> ["c", "a"]
cache.LastEvictedKey             -> "b"
cache.Evictions                  -> 1
cache.TryGet("b", out _)         -> false
cache.Hits / cache.Misses        -> 1 / 1

cache.Put("a", 99);              // update, not insert: no eviction
cache.Count                      -> 2
```

Then `LruCache.OperationsFor(int gets, int puts)` returns the number of
*pointer operations* the design performs — `2` per recency move (unlink and
relink) and `1` per dictionary write — so you can state the O(1) claim as a
number rather than a letter.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc02_collections_by_numbers review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two structures, one invariant: every key in the dictionary maps to a node
that is currently in the list, and the list's head is the most recently used.
Every operation must restore that invariant before it returns. Write it as a
comment at the top of the class and check each method against it.

## Hint 2

The recency move, which is where the O(1) lives:

```csharp
recency.Remove(node);        // O(1): the node knows its neighbours
recency.AddFirst(node);      // O(1): reuses the same node object
```

`LinkedList<T>.Remove(LinkedListNode<T>)` is the O(1) overload;
`Remove(T value)` is the O(n) one that searches. Passing the node is the whole
trick, and using the wrong overload silently turns your cache linear.

## Hint 3

Eviction happens after the insert, not before: add the new entry, then if
`Count > capacity` take `recency.Last`, remove it from both structures, record
the key and increment the counter. Decide what `Put` does when the key already
exists — the answer is "update the value and move to front, and never evict",
and the gate checks it, because an update that evicts is the classic
off-by-one in this design.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask why the array-based alternative loses here. Keeping recency in a `List<T>`
means every hit removes from the middle and appends — O(n) element moves per
*read*, on the hottest path in the cache. The linked list turns that into two
pointer writes. This is the exception that proves ex2's rule: the walk is what
was expensive, and the dictionary has removed the walk.

## Hint 2

The node carries the key as well as the value, and it has to:

```csharp
private readonly record struct Entry(TKey Key, TValue Value);
```

When you evict from the tail you have a node and need its key to remove the
dictionary entry. Storing only the value leaves you with a node you cannot
un-index, which is the bug everyone writes once.

## Hint 3

`LinkedListNode<T>.Value` is settable, so an update can reuse the node rather
than allocating a new one — worth doing, and worth noticing that it is only
possible because `Entry` is a value type you can overwrite wholesale. Count the
operations in `OperationsFor` honestly: a hit is a move (2) and no dictionary
write, a put of a new key is a dictionary write (1) plus a list insert, and an
eviction is another dictionary write plus an unlink.

lessons.title: V3·C3 — IDisposable, IAsyncDisposable and deterministic cleanup
lessons.summary: The collector decides when memory is reclaimed; you decide when everything else is. This sector is the deterministic half: the dispose pattern and when you genuinely need it, ownership and leaveOpen, IAsyncDisposable and flushing, disposal order, the exception a Dispose can hide, and unsubscribing as a resource.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·C3 — IDisposable, IAsyncDisposable and deterministic cleanup

The previous sector ended on a deliberate cliffhanger: the garbage collector
reclaims memory, eventually, on its own schedule, and that is fine for memory
and useless for everything else. A file handle held for an extra thirty
seconds blocks another process. A database connection not returned to the pool
starves the next request. A socket left open holds a port. None of those are
memory, and the collector has no opinion about any of them.

`IDisposable` is the language's answer: a convention that says "I own
something whose release cannot wait for a collection", and a `using` block
that guarantees the release happens on every path out of a scope, including
the exceptional ones.

## What `using` actually compiles to

```csharp
using (var file = File.OpenRead(path))
{
    Read(file);
}
```

becomes, near enough:

```csharp
FileStream file = File.OpenRead(path);
try
{
    Read(file);
}
finally
{
    if (file is not null) ((IDisposable)file).Dispose();
}
```

That is the entire feature. Knowing it explains everything else: why disposal
happens even when the body throws, why the `using` declaration form disposes at
the end of the *enclosing* scope, why nested `using`s dispose in reverse order
(they are nested `finally` blocks), and why an exception thrown *from* a
`Dispose` inside a `finally` replaces the exception that was already in
flight — losing the one that mattered.

## The pattern, and how little of it you usually need

The full dispose pattern — a public `Dispose()`, a `protected virtual
Dispose(bool)`, a finalizer, and `GC.SuppressFinalize` — exists for exactly one
situation: a type that directly owns an **unmanaged** resource and can be
inherited from. That is rare. The modern guidance, which the BCL follows
itself, is:

- Own unmanaged resources through a `SafeHandle`. It has a correct, robust
  finalizer already, and it is safe against being finalized in the middle of a
  P/Invoke.
- If your type only owns other `IDisposable` objects, implement `Dispose()`,
  dispose them, and write **no finalizer**. As you saw last sector, a finalizer
  makes every instance survive an extra generation for nothing.
- Seal the type if you can. Then `Dispose(bool)` is unnecessary and a plain
  private method will do.

```csharp
public sealed class Importer : IDisposable
{
    private readonly StreamReader reader;
    private bool disposed;

    public void Dispose()
    {
        if (disposed) return;   // idempotent: a second call is a no-op
        disposed = true;
        reader.Dispose();
    }
}
```

# Reading - csharp/v3cc03_deterministic_cleanup

## Notes

**`Dispose` is a promise about timing, not about memory.** Calling it does not
free the object; the collector still does that whenever it likes. What it frees
is everything the object was holding on someone else's behalf — a handle, a
lock, a pooled connection, a subscription. The test for "should this type be
disposable" is not "is it big" but "does something outside the process, or
outside this object's lifetime, notice if release is late".

**Idempotence is part of the contract.** The documented rule is that `Dispose`
may be called more than once and every call after the first must do nothing.
This is not defensive programming, it is required: `using` may dispose an
object a caller has already disposed, and `CompositeDisposable`-style
containers call it on everything they hold. A `Dispose` that throws on a second
call is a bug even if it never fires in your tests.

**The `disposing` flag means "is the rest of the world still alive".** On the
`Dispose()` path it is true and you may touch other managed objects. On the
finalizer path it is false: the objects you reference may already have been
finalized, they may be being finalized concurrently, and the thread is not
yours. Which is why the only thing a finalizer should do is release something
unmanaged, and why a `SafeHandle` doing it for you is better than doing it
yourself.

**`using` declarations dispose at the end of the enclosing scope**, not at the
end of the statement, and not where you might visually expect:

```csharp
using var connection = Open();
using var command = connection.CreateCommand();
// ...both disposed here, command first, at the closing brace of the method
```

Reverse order is a consequence of the nesting, and it matters: the command must
go before the connection it belongs to.

**A `Dispose` that throws inside a `finally` destroys evidence.** If the body
threw first, the exception from the `finally` replaces it, and the stack trace
you get points at your cleanup rather than at the failure. C# has no equivalent
of Java's suppressed-exception list, so the fix is to catch in the `finally`
yourself and combine deliberately — which is what the challenge builds.

**`IAsyncDisposable` exists because flushing is I/O.** A buffered writer's
release genuinely has to write bytes, and doing that from a synchronous
`Dispose` means blocking a thread on I/O or, worse, `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()`
on an async call — sync-over-async, the deadlock generator. `await using` gives
you the async path with the same `finally` guarantee.

**The dispose order between the two interfaces is decided by the syntax.**
`await using` prefers `DisposeAsync`; a plain `using` calls `Dispose`. A type
implementing both must make both correct, and must not implement one by
blocking on the other.

## ex1

Really testing: what each piece of the pattern is *for*. The public `Dispose`
is the caller's entry point; `Dispose(bool)` is the shared implementation;
`virtual` exists so a subclass can extend it; the finalizer is the safety net
for the unmanaged handle; `SuppressFinalize` takes a properly-disposed object
off the finalization queue. The classic mistake is a subclass overriding
`Dispose(bool)` and forgetting `base.Dispose(disposing)`, which silently leaks
the base's resources. The second is writing all of it for a type that owns only
managed objects, where the finalizer is pure cost.

## ex2

Really testing: that "disposed" is a state, not an absence.
`ObjectDisposedException.ThrowIf(disposed, this)` is the .NET 8 one-liner and
it captures the type name correctly, which matters when the exception reaches a
log. The classic mistake is only guarding some members, so a disposed object
half-works — the worst failure mode, because it produces wrong answers instead
of an exception. Note the asymmetry: every *other* member throws after
disposal, and `Dispose` itself must not.

## ex3

Really testing: ownership as an explicit decision. Wrapping a stream does not
make you its owner, and the BCL takes this so seriously that `StreamReader`,
`StreamWriter`, `BinaryReader`, `GZipStream` and `CryptoStream` all have a
`leaveOpen` constructor parameter. The classic mistake is a short-lived wrapper
closing a long-lived stream — you write a header with one writer, dispose it,
and the second writer finds a closed stream. The rule: dispose what you
created, do not dispose what you were handed, and make it a constructor
argument when the caller should choose.

## ex4

Really testing: that release can be real work. `DisposeAsync` must flush the
buffer before releasing, and it must do it exactly once — so the disposed flag
has to be set in the right place relative to the flush, or a concurrent second
call can flush a buffer that is already draining. The classic mistake is
`Dispose()` calling `DisposeAsync().GetAwaiter().GetResult()`, which blocks a
pool thread and, in a context with a synchronisation context, deadlocks
outright.

## ex5

Really testing: the two entry points and what `await using` selects. When a
type implements both, `await using` binds to `DisposeAsync` and `using` binds
to `Dispose`; the compiler does not warn you which one you got. The classic
mistake is a `using` on a type that is only `IAsyncDisposable` — that is a
compile error, which is the good case — or an `await using` on something whose
`DisposeAsync` is a lie that calls `Dispose` and returns a completed task. Also
worth noting: in library code, `DisposeAsync` should `ConfigureAwait(false)`
like any other await.

## ex6

Really testing: which exception the caller should see. When the body fails, the
body's exception is the interesting one; a disposal failure that follows is
context, not the headline. The classic mistake is the plain `try`/`finally`,
where the `finally`'s throw silently replaces the original and the stack trace
points at your cleanup code. Also being tested: reverse disposal order, and the
fact that a failure disposing the first resource must not prevent the second
from being disposed.

## ex7

Really testing: the most common managed memory leak there is. A publisher
holding a delegate holds the target object, so a long-lived event source keeps
every subscriber alive — the subscribers are unreachable from your code and
perfectly reachable from the event's invocation list. Returning an
`IDisposable` token makes unsubscribing symmetric with subscribing and gives
you `using` for scoped subscriptions. The classic mistake is unsubscribing with
a *different* delegate instance: `bus.Fired -= Handler` works because a method
group produces an equal delegate, but `-= (s, e) => ...` with a fresh lambda
removes nothing at all.

## ex8

Really testing: `Dispose` as "give it back" rather than "destroy it". A pooled
object's `Dispose` resets state and returns it, which makes `using` the natural
syntax for a rented resource. The classic mistake is the double return, which
puts one buffer in the pool twice and hands it to two owners who will
cheerfully write over each other with no exception anywhere. Detect it: a
returned buffer must know it is in the pool and refuse a second return.

## Further reading

- [Implementing a Dispose method](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/implementing-dispose) - the pattern and when the full version is needed.
- [Implementing DisposeAsync](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/implementing-disposeasync) - the async half, including the both-interfaces case.
- [SafeHandle](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.interopservices.safehandle) - why you should almost never write a finalizer.
- [ObjectDisposedException.ThrowIf](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.objectdisposedexception.throwif) - the guard, in one line.
- [using statement](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/using) - the declaration form and its scope rules.
- [Events and memory leaks](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/events/how-to-subscribe-to-and-unsubscribe-from-events) - subscription lifetime.
