# Long reading - what a throw actually does, and what it costs

## Two passes, not one

On Windows, .NET exception handling is built on Structured Exception Handling,
and SEH is a **two-pass** model. That single fact explains most of the
behaviour people find surprising.

**Pass one, the search.** Starting at the throwing frame, the runtime walks up
the stack looking for a handler willing to take this exception. For each `catch`
clause it checks the type, and if there is a `when` filter it *runs the filter*
— on the current stack, with every frame between the throw and the filter still
alive. Nothing has been unwound yet.

**Pass two, the unwind.** Once a handler is chosen, the runtime walks the stack
again, this time popping frames and running every `finally` block on the way
down, until it reaches the chosen handler, which then runs.

Consequences worth carrying:

- A `when` filter can see the world as it was at the moment of the throw. Your
  debugger's "break on unhandled exception" also works because of this: the
  decision about whether anything will handle the exception is made before any
  state is destroyed.
- A `finally` deeper in the stack runs *after* a filter higher up. Written as a
  test, that ordering looks wrong until you know about the two passes — and it
  is exactly what ex3 makes you observe.
- Filters run on a stack that has not been unwound, so a filter that throws is
  particularly nasty: that exception is swallowed and the filter is treated as
  returning false.

Unix platforms do not have SEH, and .NET implements the same semantics on top
of the platform's unwinder. The observable behaviour is identical; the
performance profile differs slightly.

## Where the microseconds go

A throw is expensive for four separate reasons, and they add up differently
depending on your code:

1. **Allocating the exception object**, which is cheap, plus whatever your
   constructor does.
2. **Capturing the stack trace.** This is the dominant cost and it scales with
   stack depth. It is captured when the exception is thrown, not when it is
   constructed — which is why `var ex = new Exception()` costs almost nothing
   and `throw ex` costs a lot.
3. **The search pass**, walking frames and consulting exception-handling
   tables, plus running filters.
4. **The unwind pass**, running `finally` blocks and popping frames.

Numbers, order of magnitude, .NET 8 on x64: a throw caught one frame away is
around 5 microseconds; twenty frames deep, several times that; across an async
state machine, more again because the exception is stored in the task, and
resurfaced with `ExceptionDispatchInfo` on the awaiting context.

Compare that to the alternatives: a `bool` return is about a nanosecond, a
`TryParse` failure tens of nanoseconds, a `Result<T>` return a few nanoseconds
plus whatever the type costs. The ratio is between a thousand and ten thousand.

That ratio is why the guidance is what it is — and why the guidance is also
*not* "avoid exceptions". At one exception per HTTP request, on a service doing
a thousand requests a second, you are spending perhaps 20 milliseconds of CPU
per second on exception handling: two percent of one core, for a mechanism that
makes failure impossible to ignore. That is a good trade. At one exception per
row of a million-row import, it is a hundred-times-worse trade and a genuine
outage risk.

## Debugger and first-chance behaviour

Every thrown exception is a **first-chance exception**: the debugger is
notified before the runtime searches for a handler. This is why a debugger
configured to break on all CLR exceptions stops on exceptions your code
catches and handles perfectly. It is also why "exceptions used as control flow"
makes debugging miserable long before it shows up in a profile — the noise
floor drowns the real failures.

In production, first-chance exceptions are visible to profilers and to ETW/
EventPipe traces. A useful diagnostic habit: if a service is slow and nobody
knows why, count first-chance exceptions. A surprisingly large fraction of
mysterious .NET performance problems turn out to be a hot path throwing and
catching thousands of exceptions a second inside a library.

## `AggregateException`, and why `await` hides it

The TPL had to solve a problem the language did not have a word for: a single
operation composed of many can fail in many ways at once.
`AggregateException` was the answer, and `Task.Wait()` and `Task.Result` throw
it, wrapping whatever went wrong — including a single failure, which is why
pre-`async` code is full of `ex.InnerException?.InnerException`.

`await` deliberately does not do that. It rethrows the *first* exception,
unwrapped, using `ExceptionDispatchInfo` so the original stack survives. That
makes ordinary code read naturally at the cost of hiding the other failures.
The other failures are not gone: `task.Exception` is still an
`AggregateException` with all of them, and `AggregateException.Flatten()`
collapses nested aggregates. If you need all of them, you must ask for them
explicitly — which ex6 makes you do.

## Cancellation, and why it wears the same clothes as failure

`OperationCanceledException` is thrown by `token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()`
and by most cancellable BCL APIs. `TaskCanceledException` derives from it and
is what task-based APIs typically throw. Catching the base type handles both.

The genuinely awkward part is that a **timeout is implemented as
cancellation**: `CancellationTokenSource.CancelAfter`, `HttpClient.Timeout` and
friends cancel a token, so the failure arrives looking identical to a caller
who pressed stop. The distinction only exists in *which* token was cancelled,
which is why the standard shape is:

```csharp
using var timeout = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
using var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(callerToken, timeout.Token);
try { await DoWork(linked.Token); }
catch (OperationCanceledException) when (callerToken.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    // the caller gave up: not an error
}
catch (OperationCanceledException)
{
    // we ran out of time: this one is an error
}
```

Getting this wrong produces one of two bad outcomes: every client disconnect
logged as an error, or every timeout logged as a client disconnect and
therefore never investigated.

## Result types: the honest trade

`Result<T>` and its relatives make expected failures cheap and explicit, and
they force callers to acknowledge the failure case. They also add ceremony to
every call site, do not compose with the BCL, cannot express "this is a bug",
and — crucially — do not remove exceptions, because the runtime still throws for
null references, division by zero, and everything underneath you.

So the defensible position is a boundary, not a replacement. Expected outcomes
inside a component return results; genuine faults throw; and exactly one place
— the controller, the message handler, the job runner — converts anything that
escapes into a response. A codebase with both channels active everywhere is
strictly worse than either alone, because every caller must handle two.

## When not to catch at all

The strongest guidance in this sector is negative. Do not catch an exception
you cannot do something specific about. A `catch` that logs and rethrows at
every layer produces five entries per failure and no more information than one.
A `catch` that converts a specific exception into a generic one destroys
information. A `catch (Exception)` at a low level turns a bug into a silent
wrong answer, which is the most expensive failure mode there is: it is found
weeks later, in data, by a customer.

Let it propagate. Somewhere near the top there is one place that knows what a
failure means for the user — return a 500, fail the message and retry later,
mark the job failed — and that is where the catching belongs.

## Exercise 1 - an exception worth catching

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC04_ExceptionDesign/Ex1.cs`.

`ImportFailedException` is a `sealed` exception with:

- the two conventional constructors: `(string message)` and
  `(string message, Exception inner)`;
- `required int Line { get; init; }` and `required string Field { get; init; }`;
- `string Describe()` returning `"line {Line}: {Field} - {Message}"`.

`ImportRules.Validate(int line, string field, string value)` throws it when a
rule fails, with the data filled in and a message that names the offending
value:

- an empty or whitespace `value` -> `"'{field}' is empty"`
- `field` is `"qty"` and `value` does not parse as a non-negative integer ->
  `"'{value}' is not a quantity"`
- `field` is `"code"` and `value` is longer than 8 characters ->
  `"'{value}' is longer than 8 characters"`

`ImportRules.ValidateAll(IEnumerable<(int Line, string Field, string Value)>
rows)` validates every row and throws a single `AggregateException` holding
every `ImportFailedException`, in row order, or returns quietly when all pass.

```
Validate(7, "qty", "-3")
  -> ImportFailedException { Line = 7, Field = "qty", Message = "'-3' is not a quantity" }
  -> Describe() == "line 7: qty - '-3' is not a quantity"

Validate(1, "code", "ABC")   // no throw
ValidateAll([(1, "qty", "x"), (2, "code", "TOO-LONG-CODE")])
  -> AggregateException with 2 inner ImportFailedExceptions, lines 1 then 2
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Design for the person catching it. They will want to know *which line* and
*which field* without parsing your sentence, so those are properties. They will
want to catch exactly this failure and not everything, so it is a specific
sealed type. The message is for a human, and it should contain the value that
caused the problem.

## Hint 2

`required` on an `init` property makes the compiler enforce what a constructor
parameter would, without a constructor explosion:

```csharp
throw new ImportFailedException($"'{value}' is not a quantity")
{
    Line = line,
    Field = field,
};
```

Omit either property at a throw site and it will not compile — which is exactly
the guarantee you want for data a caller is going to branch on.

## Hint 3

`ValidateAll` must run every row before throwing, so callers see all the
failures rather than the first. Collect into a list, and decide what to do when
that list has exactly one entry — an `AggregateException` wrapping a single
exception is still an aggregate, and choosing deliberately between "always
aggregate" and "rethrow the single one" is the design decision the gate checks.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what you would not do. You would not create a base `AppException` that
everything derives from — everyone would catch it, and it would be
`catch (Exception)` with extra ceremony. You would not put a `Code` string on it
in place of a type. Knowing the anti-designs is half of knowing the design.

## Hint 2

The message-and-inner constructor exists for wrapping, and it is not optional
even though nothing here uses it yet:

```csharp
catch (FormatException ex)
{
    throw new ImportFailedException("row could not be read", ex) { Line = n, Field = f };
}
```

Without that constructor there is no way to attach the original cause, and a
wrapper without an inner exception has destroyed the only record of what
actually failed.

## Hint 3

Write the validation rules as separate small checks in a fixed order and make
that order explicit, because a value can break more than one rule — an empty
`"qty"` is both empty and unparseable. Decide which message wins, and note that
the gate checks the message text, so "whichever check happens to be first" is
not good enough as an answer.

## Exercise 2 - guards, in one line each

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC04_ExceptionDesign/Ex2.cs`.

`Ledger.Post(string account, decimal amount, int sequence)` currently has
hand-rolled guards. Replace them with the .NET 8 helpers so that:

- `account` null throws `ArgumentNullException` with `ParamName` `"account"`;
- `account` empty or whitespace throws `ArgumentException` with the same
  `ParamName`;
- `amount` zero or negative throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` with
  `ParamName` `"amount"` and `ActualValue` equal to the amount;
- `sequence` less than the ledger's `NextSequence` throws
  `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` with `ParamName` `"sequence"`;
- posting to a disposed ledger throws `ObjectDisposedException`.

None of the guards may contain the string `"account"`, `"amount"` or
`"sequence"` as a literal — the parameter names must come from
`CallerArgumentExpression`.

Then write the domain guard:

- `Require.Balanced(decimal debits, decimal credits)` throws
  `InvalidOperationException($"unbalanced: {debits} != {credits}")` when they
  differ, and the throw itself lives in a private
  `[DoesNotReturn] static void ThrowUnbalanced(...)` so the guard stays small
  enough to inline.
- `Require.NotBlank(string? value)` throws `ArgumentException` naming the
  *caller's* expression — so `Require.NotBlank(customer.Name)` reports
  `"customer.Name"`.

```
Post(null!, 5m, 1)        -> ArgumentNullException, ParamName "account"
Post("cash", -1m, 1)      -> ArgumentOutOfRangeException, ActualValue -1
Require.NotBlank(customer.Name)  -> ArgumentException, ParamName "customer.Name"
Require.Balanced(10m, 10m)       -> no throw
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every guard you are replacing has the same three parts: a condition, an
exception type, and a parameter name. The helpers supply the second and third,
so what is left at the call site is only the condition — and often not even
that.

## Hint 2

The five you need are all static methods on the exception types themselves:

```csharp
ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(source);
ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace(name);
ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegativeOrZero(amount);
ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfLessThan(sequence, minimum);
ObjectDisposedException.ThrowIf(disposed, this);
```

Note the ordering trap: `ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace` covers null as well, so a
separate null check before it is redundant — but the *exception type* differs
(`ArgumentNullException` versus `ArgumentException`), and the gate checks
which one you produce for null.

## Hint 3

For your own helper, the attribute goes on an optional last parameter:

```csharp
public static void NotBlank(string? value,
    [CallerArgumentExpression(nameof(value))] string? expression = null)
```

The compiler fills it in with the caller's source text. Decide what to do if a
caller passes the expression explicitly — they can, it is just a parameter — and
whether that is a problem worth guarding against.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason to care is a refactor. A hand-rolled guard says
`nameof(accountId)`; someone renames the parameter to `account` and the
`nameof` follows, or does not, depending on whether they used the string form.
`CallerArgumentExpression` cannot drift, because it is captured at the call
site by the compiler.

## Hint 2

`[DoesNotReturn]` is not decoration. It tells the compiler's flow analysis that
control never comes back:

```csharp
[DoesNotReturn]
private static void ThrowUnbalanced(decimal debits, decimal credits) =>
    throw new InvalidOperationException($"unbalanced: {debits} != {credits}");
```

Without it, nullable analysis after the call assumes execution continues, and
you get spurious "may be null" warnings in the code that follows a guard.

## Hint 3

Notice why the BCL splits guards this way at all: a method containing
`throw new ...` carries the exception construction in its body, which makes it
bigger and less likely to be inlined. Moving the throw into a separate
`[DoesNotReturn]` method leaves the guard as a comparison and a call. Measure
it if you like — this is the same reasoning the benchmarking sector will teach
you to check rather than assume.

## Exercise 3 - filters decide before unwinding

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC04_ExceptionDesign/Ex3.cs`.

`TransientException(string message, int statusCode)` carries a status code as
*data*, so handlers never parse messages.

`Gateway.Call(Func<string> work, List<string> log)`:

- Runs `work` inside a `try` whose `finally` appends `"callee:finally"`.
- Catches `TransientException` **when** `StatusCode` is 500 or above, logs
  `"handled:{StatusCode}"` and returns `"retry"`.
- Any other exception, including a `TransientException` with a status below
  500, propagates untouched.
- On success returns the work's result.

`Gateway.Observe(Func<string> work, List<string> log)` demonstrates the
ordering. It calls the same inner worker directly, and its `try` has **two**
catch clauses: the first appends `"filter:evaluated"` in its filter and then
returns `false`, declining; the second is the real handler, catching a
`TransientException` of 500 or above and logging `"handled:{StatusCode}"`. A
filter on the first clause is what makes that second, more specific clause
legal.

Because filters run before the stack unwinds, the log order is:

```
Observe(() => throw new TransientException("gone", 503), log)
log -> ["filter:evaluated", "callee:finally", "handled:503"]
```

`filter:evaluated` comes **first**, before the callee's `finally`. That is the
two-pass model, observable.

```
Call(() => "ok", log)                                  -> "ok"
Call(() => throw new TransientException("x", 503), log) -> "retry"
Call(() => throw new TransientException("x", 404), log) -> throws
Call(() => throw new FormatException(), log)            -> throws
```

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc04_exception_design ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A filter answers "is this mine?" without taking the exception. If it says no,
the exception carries on completely untouched — same object, same stack trace,
still in flight — which a `catch` followed by `throw;` cannot claim, because
that one has already unwound to your frame.

## Hint 2

The filter is an expression after `when`, and it can call anything:

```csharp
catch (TransientException ex) when (ex.StatusCode >= 500)
{
    ...
}

catch (Exception ex) when (Log(ex))   // Log returns false: observe, do not handle
{
}
```

The second form is the side-effecting filter. It logs every exception passing
through this frame without catching any of them, and it is either elegant or
too clever depending on your team.

## Hint 3

To get the ordering the gate expects, the filter must be *above* the frame
containing the `finally`, and no frame in between may accept the exception
first — the search pass stops at the first clause that says yes. So put both
catch clauses in `Observe`, and let the inner worker contribute only its
`finally`. Predict the order before running it; if your prediction was wrong,
work out which pass you forgot about.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the alternative and notice what it costs:

```csharp
catch (TransientException ex)
{
    if (ex.StatusCode < 500) throw;    // already unwound; trace preserved but frames gone
    ...
}
```

This works and it has thrown away the state between the throw site and here.
With a filter, an exception you decline never knows you looked.

## Hint 2

Filter on data, never on text:

```csharp
catch (HttpRequestException ex) when (ex.StatusCode == HttpStatusCode.TooManyRequests)  // good
catch (Exception ex) when (ex.Message.Contains("timeout"))                              // fragile
```

Messages get reworded, localised, and wrapped. A status code, an error number
or an exception type does not.

## Hint 3

Watch what happens if a filter itself throws: the runtime swallows that
exception and treats the filter as having returned false. So a filter must be
cheap and total — no I/O, no allocation-heavy work, no calls that can fail.
Decide whether your `Log` helper meets that bar, and say why.

## Exercise 4 - two faces, one core

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC04_ExceptionDesign/Ex4.cs`.

A quantity is written `"12kg"`, `"500g"` or `"3lb"`, and normalises to grams.
Build both faces of the API over one core.

- `private static bool TryCore(ReadOnlySpan<char> text, out int grams, out
  string? error)` — never throws, never allocates an exception. Errors:
  `"empty"`, `"missing unit"`, `"unknown unit '{unit}'"`,
  `"'{number}' is not a number"`, `"negative"`.
- `public static int Parse(string text)` — returns the grams or throws
  `FormatException` with the core's error as its message.
- `public static bool TryParse(string? text, out int grams)` — returns false
  instead of throwing. `null` is `false`, not an `ArgumentNullException`.
- `public static int ParseOrDefault(string? text, int fallback)`.
- `Quantity.CoreCalls` and `Quantity.ExceptionsCreated` are counters the gate
  reads.

Conversions: `kg` x 1000, `g` x 1, `lb` x 454 (whole grams, truncating).

```
Parse("12kg")            -> 12000
Parse("500g")            -> 500
Parse("3lb")             -> 1362
Parse("")                -> FormatException "empty"
Parse("7stone")          -> FormatException "unknown unit 'stone'"
TryParse("nope", out _)  -> false
TryParse(null, out _)    -> false
ParseOrDefault("x", 5)   -> 5
```

The gate calls `TryParse` ten thousand times with invalid input and asserts
`ExceptionsCreated == 0`, which fails immediately for anyone who implemented
`TryParse` as `try { Parse(text); } catch { return false; }`.

```

```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the core first and give it no opinion about how failure should be
reported. It returns a bool and an error string; it does not know whether its
caller wants an exception. Both public faces are then three lines each, and the
parsing logic exists once.

## Hint 2

The two faces, once the core exists:

```csharp
public static int Parse(string text) =>
    TryCore(text, out int grams, out string? error)
        ? grams
        : throw new FormatException(error);
```

`throw` is an expression in a conditional since C# 7, which is why this fits on
one line. `TryParse` is the same call discarding the error with `out _`.

## Hint 3

Splitting the number from the unit is the only fiddly part: walk from the start
while the characters are digits, then everything after is the unit. Do it on a
`ReadOnlySpan<char>` and no substring is allocated on the failure path either —
which matters, because the whole point of the `Try` face is that failing is
cheap. Decide what `"12"` with no unit should do, and make the error message
say it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask who each face is for. `Parse` is for input you believe is valid — a config
file your deployment produced, a value you wrote — where a failure is a genuine
fault and the exception carries the diagnosis. `TryParse` is for input you
expect to be wrong sometimes: a form field, a CSV from a customer. Same logic,
different contract about whether failure is exceptional.

## Hint 2

Why catch-around-`Parse` is a bug and not a shortcut, in numbers: a throw
caught one frame away costs roughly five microseconds. Validating ten thousand
user-supplied rows where a tenth are bad is a thousand throws, so five
milliseconds of pure exception machinery — for outcomes you fully expected. The
BCL's own `int.TryParse` exists for precisely this reason.

## Hint 3

Counting is part of the exercise, so be careful where you increment.
`CoreCalls` goes up once per `TryCore` invocation, including the ones inside
`Parse` — so `Parse` must not call the core twice, which it does if you
validate first and then parse. `ExceptionsCreated` goes up where the exception
is constructed, not where it is caught; if that number is above zero on the
`TryParse` path, the implementation is wrong regardless of what it returns.

## Exercise 5 - preserving the evidence

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC04_ExceptionDesign/Ex5.cs`.

Four ways to send an exception onward, and the gate can tell them apart.

`Deep.Fail(int depth)` recurses `depth` times and then throws
`InvalidOperationException("bottom")`, so the trace has frames worth losing.

Implement `Rethrower` with four methods, each catching that exception and
sending it on differently:

- `Preserve(int depth)` — `throw;`. Same instance, trace intact, and the trace
  still names `Fail`.
- `Reset(int depth)` — `throw ex;`. Same instance, trace now starts at your
  line; `Fail` is gone from it.
- `Wrap(int depth)` — `throw new ImportFailedException("could not import", ex)
  { Line = depth, Field = "source" }`. New type, original hanging off
  `InnerException`.
- `Dispatch(int depth)` — capture with
  `ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(ex)`, return from the catch block, and throw
  it **outside** the catch. Same instance, trace preserved.

Then `TraceReport.Describe(Action work)` runs an action, catches whatever
comes out, and returns
`(string Type, string? InnerType, bool MentionsFail)` where `MentionsFail` is
whether the outermost exception's own `StackTrace` still contains `"Fail"`.

```
Describe(() => Rethrower.Preserve(5))
  -> ("InvalidOperationException", null, true)
Describe(() => Rethrower.Reset(5))
  -> ("InvalidOperationException", null, false)
Describe(() => Rethrower.Wrap(5))
  -> ("ImportFailedException", "InvalidOperationException", false)
Describe(() => Rethrower.Dispatch(5))
  -> ("InvalidOperationException", null, true)
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The question each variant answers is "what will the person reading the log
see?". `throw;` shows them where it really happened. `throw ex;` shows them
your catch block. Wrapping shows them your meaning with the truth underneath.
Dispatch is `throw;` for when you are no longer inside the catch.

## Hint 2

The two that look identical and are not:

```csharp
catch (Exception ex)
{
    throw;      // the exception in flight continues; frames below are kept
    throw ex;   // the same object, rethrown from here; StackTrace overwritten
}
```

`throw ex;` is legal, compiles without a warning in most configurations, and is
the single most common way a .NET stack trace becomes useless.

## Hint 3

`Dispatch` has a shape the others do not: capture inside the catch, throw
outside it.

```csharp
ExceptionDispatchInfo? captured = null;
try { ... } catch (Exception ex) { captured = ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(ex); }
captured?.Throw();
```

Note that the compiler cannot see that `Throw()` never returns, so you may need
a `return default;` or a `throw` after it to satisfy definite assignment.
Decide how to express "unreachable" and whether `[DoesNotReturn]` from ex2
would have helped here.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about the wrapping case as a layer boundary. Inside your import
component, a `FormatException` from a number parse is meaningful. To your
caller it is noise — they do not know you parse numbers. `ImportFailedException`
with the original inside translates without destroying, and that is the only
justification for wrapping at all.

## Hint 2

`ExceptionDispatchInfo` is not an exotic API — it is what the runtime itself
uses. When you `await` a faulted task, the exception was stored in the task
earlier, possibly on another thread, and has to be rethrown on yours with its
original trace: that is exactly `ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(...).Throw()`.
Recognising it in a stack trace ("End of stack trace from previous location")
tells you an async boundary was crossed.

## Hint 3

For `Describe`, be careful what you read. `ex.StackTrace` on the outer
exception is the outer one's trace only — an `ImportFailedException` wrapping a
deep failure has a short trace of its own, and the interesting frames are on
`ex.InnerException.StackTrace`. That distinction is why `MentionsFail` is
false for the wrapping case even though the information is not lost, and being
able to explain that sentence is the exercise.

## Exercise 6 - what async does to a failure

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC04_ExceptionDesign/Ex6.cs`.

Three things `async` changes about failure, each with a method that proves it.

- `AsyncFailures.ValidateThenWork(string? input)` is `async Task<int>` and
  validates `input` at the top with `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull`. The
  gate calls it **without awaiting** and asserts the call itself does not throw
   — the returned task is faulted instead.
- `AsyncFailures.ValidateEagerly(string? input)` is a *non-async* method that
  validates synchronously and then calls a private `async` core, so the
  argument exception is thrown at the call.
- `AsyncFailures.FirstFailureOf(params Func<Task>[] work)` awaits
  `Task.WhenAll` and returns the type name of the exception `await` produced —
  one, even when several tasks failed.
- `AsyncFailures.AllFailuresOf(params Func<Task>[] work)` returns every failure,
  in task order, as a list of type names, by reading the aggregated task's
  `Exception` rather than relying on `await`.

```
Task<int> t = ValidateThenWork(null);      // no throw here
t.IsFaulted                                 -> true (after it completes)
await t                                     -> throws ArgumentNullException

ValidateEagerly(null)                       -> throws ArgumentNullException immediately

await FirstFailureOf(Boom<FormatException>, Boom<OverflowException>)
  -> "FormatException"
await AllFailuresOf(Boom<FormatException>, Boom<OverflowException>)
  -> ["FormatException", "OverflowException"]
```

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc04_exception_design ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An `async` method's body runs inside a state machine, and everything that
escapes it — including code before the first `await` — is captured into the
returned task rather than thrown at the caller. That is the whole of the first
surprise, and it explains why the BCL splits validation out of `async` methods
so often.

## Hint 2

The eager-validation split, which is the standard fix:

```csharp
public static Task<int> ValidateEagerly(string? input)
{
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(input);    // throws at the call site
    return Core(input);

    static async Task<int> Core(string text) { await Task.Yield(); return text.Length; }
}
```

The outer method is not `async`, so its throw is synchronous; the inner local
function carries the awaits.

## Hint 3

For the aggregate, remember that `await` unwraps to the *first* exception while
the task keeps all of them:

```csharp
Task all = Task.WhenAll(tasks);
try { await all; }
catch { /* one exception */ }
AggregateException? every = all.Exception;   // all of them, flattened with Flatten()
```

Decide whether to read `all.Exception` after catching, or to inspect each task
individually — both work, and only one keeps the original task order reliably.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what a caller can even do with a faulted task they never awaited. Nothing
useful — and if they abandon it, the exception used to crash the process on
finalization and now goes quietly unobserved. That is the practical reason
argument validation should be eager: the failure reaches the caller at the
moment they made the mistake.

## Hint 2

The two entry points look identical from outside and differ in one keyword:

```csharp
public static async Task<int> A(string? s) { ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(s); ... }
public static Task<int> B(string? s)       { ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(s); ... }
```

`A` returns a faulted task; `B` throws. Neither is wrong in general — but for
argument validation the second is the documented convention, and for anything
that happens *during* the operation the first is correct.

## Hint 3

`AggregateException.Flatten()` matters more than it looks. `Task.WhenAll` over
tasks that themselves came from `WhenAll` gives you nested aggregates, and
`InnerExceptions` on the outer one then contains aggregates rather than the
real failures. Flatten first, then read, and decide whether your ordering
guarantee survives it — it may be safer to walk the original tasks.

## Exercise 7 - cancellation is not failure

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC04_ExceptionDesign/Ex7.cs`.

A caller giving up and an operation running out of time both arrive as
`OperationCanceledException`. Tell them apart.

`Outcome` is `"completed"`, `"cancelled"`, `"timedout"` or `"failed"`.

`Caller.Run(Func<CancellationToken, Task<string>> work, TimeSpan timeout,
CancellationToken callerToken)` returns `(Outcome Outcome, string? Value,
string? Error)`:

- Creates a timeout source with `CancelAfter` and links it to `callerToken`
  with `CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource`.
- Passes the **linked** token to `work`.
- On success: `("completed", value, null)`.
- On `OperationCanceledException` when `callerToken.IsCancellationRequested`:
  `("cancelled", null, null)` — a caller giving up is not an error, so there
  is no message.
- On `OperationCanceledException` otherwise: `("timedout", null, $"timed out
  after {timeout.TotalMilliseconds:0}ms")`.
- On any other exception: `("failed", null, ex.Message)`.
- Both cancellation token sources are disposed.

`Caller.ShouldLogAsError(Outcome outcome)` returns true only for `"failed"` and
`"timedout"`.

```
Run(ct => Task.FromResult("ok"), 1s, none)             -> ("completed", "ok", null)
Run(ct => Forever(ct), 50ms, none)                      -> ("timedout", null, "timed out after 50ms")
Run(ct => Forever(ct), 10s, alreadyCancelledToken)      -> ("cancelled", null, null)
Run(ct => throw new IOException("disk"), 1s, none)      -> ("failed", null, "disk")
ShouldLogAsError("cancelled")                           -> false
```

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc04_exception_design ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The exception type cannot tell you what happened, because both causes throw the
same type. The *token* can: after catching, ask whether the caller's token is
the one that was cancelled. That single question is the whole exercise, and it
is why the linked source exists.

## Hint 2

The standard shape, with filters doing the classification:

```csharp
using var timeout = new CancellationTokenSource(duration);
using var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(callerToken, timeout.Token);
try { return await work(linked.Token); }
catch (OperationCanceledException) when (callerToken.IsCancellationRequested) { ... }
catch (OperationCanceledException) { /* must have been the timeout */ }
```

Order matters: the caller's cancellation is checked first, because if both
happened at once, the caller's intent is the more useful explanation.

## Hint 3

`TaskCanceledException` derives from `OperationCanceledException`, so catching
the base handles both — and catching only `TaskCanceledException` misses
cancellations raised by `token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()`. Decide what
`Run` should do if `work` ignores the token and completes normally after the
timeout fired: the token was cancelled, but nothing threw, and returning
`"completed"` is defensible if you can say why.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the dashboard. Every client that closes a browser tab cancels a
request; if those are logged as errors, your error rate is a measure of user
impatience and nobody trusts it any more. Getting this classification right is
the difference between an alert that means something and one everybody mutes.

## Hint 2

Disposal matters here for a specific reason: a `CancellationTokenSource` with a
timer holds an entry in the timer queue, and a linked source registers a
callback on every token it links. Neither is released until you dispose:

```csharp
using var timeout = new CancellationTokenSource(duration);
using var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(a, b);
```

Two `using` declarations, disposed in reverse — the sector on deterministic
cleanup, showing up in the middle of an exception exercise.

## Hint 3

Think about what `Error` should contain in each case. For `"failed"` it is the
exception's message, because someone will need it. For `"timedout"` it is the
duration, because the exception's message ("A task was canceled.") tells nobody
anything. For `"cancelled"` it is null, because there is nothing to explain.
Three different answers to "what should the log line say" is the design content
of this exercise.

## Exercise 8 - results at the edge

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC04_ExceptionDesign/Ex8.cs`.

Expected failures return; genuine faults throw; exactly one place converts
between the two.

`readonly record struct Result<T>`:

- `static Result<T> Ok(T value)` and `static Result<T> Fail(string error)`.
- `bool IsOk`, `T? Value`, `string? Error`.
- `Result<TNext> Map<TNext>(Func<T, TNext> map)` — maps on success, passes the
  error through on failure, and never invokes `map` on a failure.
- `T ValueOrThrow()` — the deliberate conversion back to an exception.

`Rules.Check(string code, int quantity)` returns `Result<Order>`, using
failures for the expected cases — an empty code, a quantity outside 1..999 —
and no exceptions at all.

`Edge.Handle(Func<Result<Order>> operation)` is the boundary. It returns
`(int Status, string Body)`:

- a successful result -> `(200, order.Code)`;
- a failed result -> `(400, error)`;
- an exception escaping `operation` -> `(500, "internal error")`, and the
  exception's message is *not* leaked to the body.

`Rules.ExceptionsCreated` counts exception constructions so the gate can hold
the expected path to zero.

```
Rules.Check("A1", 5)        -> Ok, Order("A1", 5)
Rules.Check("", 5)          -> Fail "code is required"
Rules.Check("A1", 0)        -> Fail "quantity must be between 1 and 999"
Edge.Handle(() => Rules.Check("A1", 5))   -> (200, "A1")
Edge.Handle(() => Rules.Check("", 5))     -> (400, "code is required")
Edge.Handle(() => throw new IOException("disk /dev/sda1 offline"))
  -> (500, "internal error")
```

The gate runs ten thousand invalid checks and asserts `ExceptionsCreated == 0`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc04_exception_design ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The design rule is about *where*, not *whether*. Inside the component,
expected failures are values. At the edge — one method — anything that escaped
becomes a status code. A codebase with both channels active everywhere is
worse than either alone, because every caller has to handle two.

## Hint 2

`Map` is what makes results composable rather than a nest of `if`s:

```csharp
Result<string> name = Rules.Check(code, qty).Map(order => order.Code);
```

The important part is that `map` is not called on the failure path — so a
chain of five maps over a failed result does no work at all and carries the
original error to the end.

## Hint 3

`Edge.Handle` is the only place with a `catch`, and it should catch broadly
*and* say so. Note what it must not do: put `ex.Message` in the body. A message
like `"disk /dev/sda1 offline"` tells an attacker about your infrastructure,
and tells the user nothing they can act on. Log it, return a generic body, and
decide whether to include a correlation id — that is the design decision the
gate is silent about and a reviewer would not be.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask which failures belong in which channel before you write anything. A
quantity of zero is expected — a user typed it. A disk going offline is not.
The test is not severity, it is whether the caller could have prevented it and
whether it happens routinely.

## Hint 2

`Result<T>` as a `readonly record struct` gives you equality, deconstruction
and no heap allocation, which is what makes the expected-failure path cheap:

```csharp
public readonly record struct Result<T>(bool IsOk, T? Value, string? Error);
```

If it were a class, ten thousand failures would be ten thousand allocations —
better than ten thousand exceptions, still worse than none.

## Hint 3

`ValueOrThrow` is the one place inside the component that converts back, and
it should be rare enough to notice. Decide what exception it throws — a
generic `InvalidOperationException` with the error as its message is the usual
answer — and be able to explain why calling it in a loop would undo everything
the type was for.

## Challenge - classify, then retry only what is retryable

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC04_ExceptionDesign/Challenge.cs`.

`FailurePipeline.RunAsync(IReadOnlyList<Func<int, CancellationToken,
Task<string>>> items, RetryPolicy policy, CancellationToken ct)` processes
every item, retrying the failures that deserve it.

`RetryPolicy(int MaxAttempts, int BaseDelayMs, int MaxDelayMs)` — the backoff
schedule is deterministic and computed, not slept: attempt `n` (1-based) waits
`min(BaseDelayMs * 2^(n-1), MaxDelayMs)` milliseconds, and the pipeline
**records** the schedule rather than sleeping, so the gate can assert it.

Classification, in this order:

1. `OperationCanceledException` with `ct` cancelled -> `Cancelled`. Never
   retried; the pipeline stops immediately and returns what it has.
2. `TransientException` with `StatusCode >= 500`, or `TimeoutException` ->
   `Transient`. Retried until `MaxAttempts` is reached.
3. Anything else -> `Permanent`. Never retried.

`PipelineReport`:

- `IReadOnlyList<string> Succeeded` — the values, in item order.
- `IReadOnlyList<int> DelaysMs` — every delay the schedule called for, in
  order, across all items.
- `int Attempts` — total invocations of any item.
- `AggregateException? Permanent` — every permanent failure, in item order,
  or null when there were none. Transient failures that exhausted their
  attempts are permanent failures too.
- `bool Cancelled`.

```
policy = new RetryPolicy(MaxAttempts: 3, BaseDelayMs: 100, MaxDelayMs: 500)

item succeeds on attempt 3 after two 5xx failures
  -> Succeeded ["ok"], DelaysMs [100, 200], Attempts 3, Permanent null

item always throws TransientException(503)
  -> Attempts 3, DelaysMs [100, 200], Permanent holds the last TransientException

item throws FormatException
  -> Attempts 1, DelaysMs [], Permanent holds the FormatException

caller cancels during item 2 of 4
  -> Cancelled true, items 3 and 4 never attempted
```

Honest difficulty note: the retry loop is ten lines and the *classification* is
the exercise. Write the three rules down, in order, before writing any code —
and note that rule 1 is checked before rule 2, so a cancellation that arrives
dressed as a timeout is still a cancellation.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc04_exception_design challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Separate the two jobs completely. One function classifies an exception into
`Cancelled`, `Transient` or `Permanent` and does nothing else. Another runs the
loop and consults it. Mixing them gives you a `catch` chain that is also a
policy, which is unreadable and untestable.

## Hint 2

The schedule is arithmetic, so it needs no clock:

```csharp
static int DelayFor(RetryPolicy policy, int attempt) =>
    Math.Min(policy.BaseDelayMs * (1 << (attempt - 1)), policy.MaxDelayMs);
```

Recording the delays instead of sleeping is what makes the whole pipeline
testable in microseconds. A production version would `await
Task.Delay(delay, ct)` at the same point — and note that the `ct` there is what
makes a cancellation interrupt a backoff rather than waiting it out.

## Hint 3

The last attempt has no delay after it — a schedule of `[100, 200]` for three
attempts, not `[100, 200, 400]` — because you only wait when you are about to
try again. Off by one here is the most common bug in retry code, closely
followed by counting attempts as retries. Decide which you are counting, name
the variable accordingly, and the arithmetic stops fighting you.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what makes a failure retryable. Not its type, exactly: a 500 is retryable
and a 400 is not, though both are `HttpRequestException`. Retryability is
"would doing exactly this again plausibly succeed?" — which is a property of
the *cause*, and is why the classification needs structured data rather than a
type test.

## Hint 2

Retrying the wrong thing is worse than not retrying. A 400 retried three times
is three times the load for three identical failures; a non-idempotent request
retried after a timeout may run twice on the server. State that assumption:
this pipeline retries only operations that are safe to repeat, and a real one
would carry an idempotency key.

## Hint 3

Cancellation deserves its own path, not a `catch` at the end. When the caller's
token fires, the correct behaviour is to stop the whole pipeline — not to mark
this item failed and move on to the next one, which would do exactly the work
the caller asked you to abandon. Return what has succeeded so far, flag
`Cancelled`, and leave the remaining items untouched.

## Review 1 - what does the caller actually see?

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CC04_ExceptionDesign/Review1.cs`. The sector from the
caller's side: given handling code, predict the exception a caller observes,
then fix the version that destroyed the evidence.

`Layers` contains three stacked layers, supplied:

- `Storage.Read(string key)` throws `KeyNotFoundException($"no row '{key}'")`.
- `Repository.Load(string key)` catches it and wraps:
  `new ImportFailedException($"could not load '{key}'", inner) { Line = 0,
  Field = key }`.
- `Service.Fetch(string key)` catches `ImportFailedException` and wraps again:
  `new InvalidOperationException("fetch failed", inner)`.

Implement:

- `ChainReport.Of(Action work)` — runs the action and returns the observed
  chain as a list of `"{TypeName}: {Message}"`, outermost first, walking
  `InnerException` to the bottom.
- `ChainReport.Depth(Exception exception)` — how many exceptions are in the
  chain.
- `ChainReport.Root(Exception exception)` — the innermost exception, which is
  what actually went wrong.

Then the fix:

- `BrokenService.Fetch(string key)` is supplied and uses `throw ex;` inside its
  catch, resetting the trace.
- `FixedService.Fetch(string key)` must produce the identical exception chain
  while preserving the original stack trace, so
  `ChainReport.MentionsStorage(exception)` — whether the outermost exception's
  own `StackTrace` names `Storage` — is true for `FixedService` and false for
  `BrokenService`.

```
ChainReport.Of(() => Service.Fetch("x"))
  -> ["InvalidOperationException: fetch failed",
      "ImportFailedException: could not load 'x'",
      "KeyNotFoundException: no row 'x'"]

ChainReport.Depth(caught)   -> 3
ChainReport.Root(caught)    -> the KeyNotFoundException
ChainReport.MentionsStorage(fromBroken) -> false
ChainReport.MentionsStorage(fromFixed)  -> true
```

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cc04_exception_design review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the three layers as a story and write the answer down before you run
anything. Each layer adds a sentence and keeps the previous one underneath, so
the chain is a narrative from "what the user asked for" at the top to "what
actually happened" at the bottom. That is what wrapping is *for*.

## Hint 2

Walking the chain is a `while` loop, and the null check is the terminator:

```csharp
for (Exception? current = exception; current is not null; current = current.InnerException)
{
    yield return $"{current.GetType().Name}: {current.Message}";
}
```

Note that `AggregateException` does not fit this shape — it has many inners, not
one — so a general-purpose version would need to branch. Say whether yours
does.

## Hint 3

For the fix, ask what `BrokenService` actually loses. Its chain is identical;
what changed is the outermost exception's own `StackTrace`, which now begins in
the catch block rather than naming the frames below. Getting `MentionsStorage`
to be true means the exception must reach the caller without being rethrown
from a different line — which leaves you one choice from ex5, and you should be
able to say which and why.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what each layer is entitled to say. `Storage` knows about rows.
`Repository` knows about imports. `Service` knows about fetches. Each wrap
translates into the vocabulary of the next caller up — and each one that
discards the inner exception deletes a chapter of the explanation.

## Hint 2

Three wraps is arguably two too many. In real code the rule is to wrap at
*boundaries* — where the vocabulary genuinely changes, usually a public API
surface — and to let the exception through everywhere else:

```csharp
catch (KeyNotFoundException ex)
{
    throw new ImportFailedException($"could not load '{key}'", ex) { ... };
}
```

Wrapping at every layer produces chains of five where three carry no
information, and a log entry nobody reads to the bottom of.

## Hint 3

`Root` is more useful than it looks: alerting and grouping should key off the
innermost exception's type, because that is the thing that actually failed.
Two outages with identical outer types and different roots are different
outages. Implement it as a walk to the last non-null `InnerException`, and
decide what it should return for an exception with no inner at all.
